The door has held for a hundred years. Tonight, someone on the other side is knocking. Your companions look at you. You have a lantern, a scar that aches before rain, and one very bad idea that might get everyone through this alive.

Heroes of Legend is a fantasy roleplaying game about people who become remarkable through the choices they make. You might be a scholar who reads an opponent's stance like a page, a guardian who plants a shield in the only safe doorway, or a wanderer who calls the forest to your friends' defense. Your character is built from ancestry, experience, class and learned abilities. The combinations belong to you.

Each player speaks and acts for one hero. One participant is the Dungeon Architect, or DA: the person who describes the world, portrays the people and creatures in it, presents danger, and adjudicates uncertain situations. The DA tells you what your hero can perceive. You say what you try. Together, you discover what happens.

The door has held for a hundred years. Tonight, someone on the other side is knocking. Your companions look at you. You have a lantern, a scar that aches before rain, and one very bad idea that might get everyone through this alive.

Heroes of Legend is a fantasy roleplaying game about people who become remarkable through the choices they make. You might be a scholar who reads an opponent's stance like a page, a guardian who plants a shield in the only safe doorway, or a wanderer who calls the forest to your friends' defense. Your character is built from ancestry, experience, class and learned abilities. The combinations belong to you.

At the table

Each player speaks and acts for one hero. One participant is the Dungeon Architect, or DA: the person who describes the world, portrays the people and creatures in it, presents danger, and adjudicates uncertain situations. The DA tells you what your hero can perceive. You say what you try. Together, you discover what happens.

You do not need to act in a voice, memorize this book, or find a single correct solution. Ask questions. Describe a practical approach. Listen to what your companions want to attempt. A good plan can change the situation before anyone touches a die.

You will need three six-sided dice, and ideally three more for Boons and Banes. Consumable supplies use d4, d6, d8, d10, d12 and d20 inventory dice. Bring a character sheet, your learned abilities, something to record changes, and tokens or miniatures when a scene benefits from a square grid. A virtual tabletop can do the same work.

The promise of the game

Choose what your hero practices and how you want to help your companions. Study disciplines to learn techniques and spells. When you use one, its entry tells you the action to spend, the attribute to roll, its range and what each result does. Your sword's appearance is yours to invent; the attack describes what it accomplishes.

Attacks connect. A poor roll changes how much harm and pressure an attack creates; it does not usually erase the turn. A stronger result may push an enemy away, expose a weakness, leave them burning, or put an ally where they need to be.

You recover HP through healing and rest. Scars and spent Grit follow you. Victories can leave permanent scars. A hero who rises again is not untouched by what happened.

Learn one roll

When an uncertain action has consequences, roll 3d6 + one attribute. The six attributes are Brawn, Fortitude, Agility, Guile, Knowledge and Reason. An ability names its attribute; otherwise the DA calls for the attribute that fits the attempt.

TotalResultWhat it means
8 or lessWeakMake the printed progress; you have not necessarily completed your purpose.
9–14StandardApply the Standard outcome.
15 or moreStrongApply the Strong outcome.

Three retained natural ones give Weak plus a complication. Three retained natural sixes give Strong plus a benefit. These exceptional results use the numbers on the dice, before adding your attribute.

Boons help and Banes hinder. Cancel one against one. Each remaining Boon adds a die; keep the highest three. Each remaining Bane adds a die; keep the lowest three. Use at most three net extra dice. Add your attribute after choosing the three dice. Difficulty changes the dice you keep, not the Weak/Standard/Strong boundaries.

> Example — a dangerous crossing. Lira has Agility +2. The DA asks for Agility > to cross a crumbling beam before the pursuers arrive. The rotten surface adds > 1 Bane; an ally's secured rope supplies 1 Boon. They cancel. Lira rolls 2, 4, 5: > 11 + 2 = 13, a Standard result. She reaches the far ledge as agreed before the roll. > If there were no danger or meaningful cost, the group could simply describe crossing.

A moment of play

DA: The broken bridge ends two squares short of the far bank. Water roars below. The rider behind you is reaching for a horn.

Lira: I have room to run. Can I jump the gap?

DA: Your Agility is +2, so your running broad jump reaches four squares. There is a clear landing. Spend the movement and you are across; no roll needed.

Borin: I cannot leave Oren behind. I plant myself between him and the rider. I use Defend and keep my Reaction ready.

Oren: I use Force on the jammed bridge mechanism. Can we lower the remaining span?

DA: Yes. It needs two progress. A Weak result loosens it, but the rider will have time to sound the horn. A Standard or Strong result opens it now.

Oren: Brawn +0. I roll 3, 4, 5: twelve. Standard, two progress.

DA: The catch tears loose. The span drops with a crack, giving you a route across. The rider lowers the horn and draws a blade instead.

This is play: make choices in the fiction, apply the rule that fits, and let the result change what can happen next. Force is an action Oren chooses. Brawn is the attribute the action tells him to roll.

Find your way through the book

Read Create Your Hero to build from the beginning, or choose one of the six ready-to-play heroes near the back. Ancestries, origins and classes supply your first choices. Disciplines show how to qualify for learned abilities. Playing the Game explains combat; Beyond the Battlefield covers the rest of an adventurer's life.

Keep your own abilities close at hand. Use the Basic Actions chapter for things any hero can do, and check each action for any gear you need. When you want to try something the book does not list, describe it to the DA so they can make a ruling.

Before the first adventure

Agree on the tone of the campaign and why your heroes travel together. Discuss what kinds of danger, injury and horror people want included or left offstage. Anyone can ask to pause a scene or change an uncomfortable detail. Surviving at 0 leaves a player-chosen descriptive scar, without mechanical penalties.

Choose names, something each hero wants, and a connection between companions. Decide how to share maps and record supplies. The DA should explain what your characters already know about the first destination. You can discover the rest in play.

Assign a value from −2 to +2 to each of the six attributes. Their total must be +3. A straightforward starting array is +2, +1, +1, +0, +0, −1, arranged as you choose. Check your intended class's minimums before settling the array.

These are not exclusive lists. Roll the attribute printed on the ability you use. Some techniques deliberately use an unusual attribute, such as Knowledge for a carefully studied attack. There is no added skill rating.

Your chosen attributes stay fixed as you gain levels. Use those values for creation DP and class eligibility. An item can change your effective attribute while its rules apply, even outside the creation range. Assign attributes

Assign a value from −2 to +2 to each of the six attributes. Their total must be +3. A straightforward starting array is +2, +1, +1, +0, +0, −1, arranged as you choose. Check your intended class's minimums before settling the array.

AttributeCommon uses
BrawnExert strength, use Force, climb and make many melee attacks.
FortitudeEndure harm, resist bodily threats and make death rolls; contributes to HP.
AgilityMove deftly, remain Hidden, jump and make many ranged attacks; contributes to Speed.
GuileDeceive, misdirect, improvise and exploit an opening.
KnowledgeApply learning, recognize patterns, craft and use learned techniques.
ReasonNotice details, perceive danger, judge a situation and keep your thinking clear.

These are not exclusive lists. Roll the attribute printed on the ability you use. Some techniques deliberately use an unusual attribute, such as Knowledge for a carefully studied attack. There is no added skill rating.

Your chosen attributes stay fixed as you gain levels. Use those values for creation DP and class eligibility. An item can change your effective attribute while its rules apply, even outside the creation range. See @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.fe4cfea054174e98]{Equipment and Recipes} for bonuses, penalties, and items that set an attribute to a specific value.

Choose ancestry

Choose one ancestry and two of its five traits. Record the described characteristic, benefit and any side effect together. Ancestry contributes HP each level and SP and coins once at creation. Any ancestry can grow up in any culture and follow any class whose requirements the character meets.

Create a level-1 hero

Assign Brawn, Fortitude, Agility, Guile, Knowledge and Reason from -2 through +2, totaling +3. Attributes stay fixed as you gain levels. Choose an ancestry and two of its five traits. Record the characteristic and its benefits and side effects together.

Choose a culture and background independently of ancestry. Each offers two disciplines; begin studying one from each. Choose a class whose attribute minimums you meet, then begin studying one discipline from its starting list. Choose three distinct disciplines across these choices. Select one level-1 class signature.

Your starting Development Points (DP) are 10 + Guile + Knowledge + Reason, including negative values, plus explicit trait benefits. Use these points to learn abilities and spellbook sections. Starting disciplines are already yours to study. An additional discipline costs the 1, 2 or 3 DP printed for your class; then learn its entries at their listed prices. Save unspent DP for later development.

Learning your paths

Choose a path in a discipline you study. Begin with its first entry and follow the path in order. Check the level and DP listed at each entry. If a technique has an improvement, keep its earlier benefits unless the new entry replaces one.

To learn spells, choose a spellbook and study its sections in order. Each section teaches the spells marked with that number. Your learned spells remain available whenever you can pay their casting cost. The first spell in each book costs 0 SP. See @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.684bcf0a86d4b4b4]{Magic and spellbooks} for the full procedure.

Every hero can use basic actions such as melee and ranged attacks, Aid, Stabilize and Sustain Spell. Check the action for any gear it requires.

Signatures

Choose one signature at each of levels 1, 3 and 7 without spending DP. Choose from your class’s options for that level. Each signature is an ability you can use in its own right. Some offer an additional benefit when you also know another named signature; that benefit appears in the ability’s rules.

You may change a signature selection. Choose a replacement from the same milestone and update any benefits that depend on knowing both signatures. Each earned milestone still supplies one selection; changing it neither spends nor grants DP, repeats an acquisition benefit, nor restores used resources.

Equipment and starting numbers

Take the ordinary weapons, ammunition, armor, instrument, and other ordinary gear your learned abilities require, free of charge. One compatible item serves every ability that can use it. A plain worn outfit is free.

> Starting coins\ > 40 + ancestry + culture + background + class coin contributions

Begin with a Food Bundle, Water Flask, Lighting Bundle, and Lesser Healing Bottle. Pay their listed prices from your starting coins. Return any you do not want before completing creation and recover its full cost. After creation, use the ordinary sale and trade rules. Spend any remaining coins on other gear.

> Maximum HP\ > 10 + level × (ancestry HP + class HP) + Fortitude + fixed benefits

Begin with full HP. Count Fortitude and fixed benefits once.

> Maximum SP\ > 2 × level + ancestry SP + 2 × positive class casting attribute + Spellcraft bonuses + other SP bonuses

Your level contributes 2 SP at level 1 and 2 more at each later level. Add twice your class’s casting attribute if it is positive. Spellcraft bonuses come from the Soul Capacity and Mind Capacity paths in the Spellcraft discipline. The first entry in each path adds 2 maximum SP to the same reserve. Begin with full SP. See @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.d7def8e34dfcb560]{Starting SP} for the class attributes and examples.

> Capacity\ > 10 + 3 × Brawn

> Speed\ > Ancestry base Speed + Agility + applicable trait bonuses − 1 per Bulk above Capacity. Minimum 0.

> Stability and resistance\ > Stability starts at 0. Use the highest explicit source of Stability and the highest matching resistance. Each has a maximum of 3. Apply damage immunity before resistance.

> Grit\ > Gain 1 Grit at levels 1, 3 and 7. Spend each point once. When you spend Grit, return to half maximum HP, rounded up.

Record current HP and SP, first-aid availability, death tallies and scars separately. See @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.9303127ab1b28c3b]{recovery}.

Advancement

The DA awards milestone levels. Apply these gains each time you reach a new level after level 1.

> DP gained\ > 6 + your new level, plus explicit trait benefits.

Save the points or spend them when the DA judges you are somewhere safe.

> HP gained\ > Add your ancestry HP + class HP to maximum HP. If you have positive HP, add the same amount to current HP. At 0 HP, increase only your maximum.

> SP at a new level\ > Add 2 to maximum SP. Keep your current SP at its previous value. If you have 3 / 8 SP before reaching level 2, you have 3 / 10 SP afterward. A safe overnight rest fills your reserve to 10 / 10 SP.

Neither a level gain nor a signature change refreshes spent Grit.

Record what you learned and the DP you spent. At level 3 you can learn advanced entries, and at level 7 you can learn masteries. Follow each path’s order and pay the listed costs.

Introduction

Your level contributes twice its value in Spell Points: 2 SP at level 1, 6 at level 3 and 14 at level 7. Add SP from your ancestry, class and any capacity or benefits you learned. Calculate the reserve after making your creation choices, then begin with that many SP. Record learned spells alongside the reserve.

Maximum SP

2 × level + ancestry SP + 2 × positive class casting attribute + Spellcraft bonuses + other SP bonuses

A class attribute of 0 or less contributes 0. Use your base value for the class’s casting attribute. Ancestry, class and learned bonuses are added once. The level contribution grows by 2 SP each level.

Learned capacity and recovery

Soul Capacity and Mind Capacity are paths in the Spellcraft discipline. Both increase the same reserve. Soul Capacity I and Mind Capacity I each add 2 maximum SP. Add each learned increase once, using the amount printed for that entry. Recovery restores spent SP through its named rest activity. Channeling transfers existing SP between reserves. Learning a new entry or raising maximum SP after creation does not itself refill the reserve.

Growth and examples

At each level after 1, increase your maximum SP by 2. Keep your current SP at its previous value. For example, a hero with 3 / 8 SP reaches level 2 with 3 / 10 SP. A safe overnight rest fills the new reserve. These gains add up to 4 more maximum SP at level 3 and 12 more at level 7, before additional learned benefits.

Hill Dwarf Protector, Reason +1: 2 × 1 level + 0 ancestry + 2 class = 4 SP at level 1. At level 3, the reserve is 8 SP before learned capacity.

High Elf Arcanist, Knowledge +2: 2 × 1 level + 2 ancestry + 4 class = 8 SP at level 1. Learning Soul Capacity I adds 2, making 10 SP. At level 7 with that same learning, the reserve is 22 SP.

Current and maximum SP

Record current SP separately. Pay a spell's printed SP when casting; each book's first spell costs 0 SP. Sustain uses a Maneuver and 0 SP. A Brief Rest restores 3 SP once per day. A Night’s Rest fills your reserve. Other recovery and transfer follow their listed time and limits.

Create a level-1 hero

Assign Brawn, Fortitude, Agility, Guile, Knowledge and Reason from -2 through +2, totaling +3. Attributes stay fixed as you gain levels. Choose an ancestry and two of its five traits. Record the characteristic and its benefits and side effects together.

Choose a culture and background independently of ancestry. Each offers two disciplines; begin studying one from each. Choose a class whose attribute minimums you meet, then begin studying one discipline from its starting list. Choose three distinct disciplines across these choices. Select one level-1 class signature.

Your starting Development Points (DP) are 10 + Guile + Knowledge + Reason, including negative values, plus explicit trait benefits. Use these points to learn abilities and spellbook sections. Starting disciplines are already yours to study. An additional discipline costs the 1, 2 or 3 DP printed for your class; then learn its entries at their listed prices. Save unspent DP for later development.

Learning your paths

Choose a path in a discipline you study and learn its entries in order. Pay each entry’s DP cost and meet its level requirement. Advanced entries become available at level 3 and mastery at level 7. Apply improvements together unless an entry replaces a previous value. You can study several paths.

In the discipline atlas, circles mark level-1 entries, triangles mark level-3 entries, and diamonds mark level-7 entries. Solid gold shows an entry you know. A gold border around green shows one you can learn now. Follow the lines to see what comes next.

Choose a spellbook in a magical discipline you study. Learn its sections in order and add the spells marked with that section number. Keep the spells you learn, and cast each for its printed SP cost. The first spell in each book costs 0 SP. In Spellcraft, Soul Capacity and Mind Capacity increase your maximum SP, Recovery restores spent SP, and Channeling lets you transfer SP.

Every hero can use the basic actions, including melee and ranged attacks, Aid, Stabilize and Sustain Spell.

Signatures

Choose one signature at each of levels 1, 3 and 7 without spending DP. Choose from your class’s options for that level. Each signature is an ability you can use in its own right. Some offer an additional benefit when you also know another named signature; that benefit appears in the ability’s rules.

You may change a signature selection. Choose a replacement from the same milestone and update any benefits that depend on knowing both signatures. Each earned milestone still supplies one selection; changing it neither spends nor grants DP, repeats an acquisition benefit, nor restores used resources.

Equipment and starting numbers

Take compatible ordinary equipment required by your learned techniques for free. One item can serve several compatible techniques. A plain worn outfit is free. From 40 + ancestry + culture + background + class coin contributions, pay for starting food, water, lighting and a lesser healing potion. Return unwanted starting provisions at their full price before finishing creation. Spend the balance on other gear. Light, medium and heavy armor grant physical resistance 1, 2 and 3 while worn. If you lack the matching training, subtract that suit’s rating from effective Agility.

Maximum HP is 10 + level x (ancestry HP contribution + class HP contribution) + Fortitude + fixed benefits. Begin with full HP. Each later level adds ancestry + class contributions to maximum HP; Fortitude and fixed benefits apply once. When you have positive HP, add that level's HP gain to current HP too. At 0 HP, only maximum HP grows.

Maximum SP is 2 × level + ancestry SP + 2 × positive class casting attribute + Spellcraft bonuses + other SP bonuses. Spellcraft bonuses come from its Soul Capacity and Mind Capacity paths. Add other SP bonuses only when a rule explicitly grants them. A class attribute of 0 or less adds 0 SP. Use your base value for the class’s casting attribute. Begin with your full reserve. Later maximum-SP gains enlarge capacity without restoring spent points. Safe overnight rest restores the reserve.

Capacity is 10 + 3 x Brawn. Every Bulk above capacity reduces Speed by 1. Speed is ancestry base + Agility - encumbrance, minimum 0. Stability starts at 0; use the highest explicit source, maximum 3. Matching resistance uses the highest value, maximum 3. Damage immunity removes its named damage before resistance.

Gain 1 Grit at level 1, 1 at level 3 and 1 at level 7. Each point can be used once and is gone permanently. Using Grit restores you to half maximum HP, rounded up. Record current HP/SP, first-aid availability, death tallies and scars separately. See @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.9303127ab1b28c3b]{recovery}.

Advancement

The DA awards milestone levels. From level 2 onward, gain 6 + the new level DP, plus explicit trait benefits. Save points or spend them when the DA judges you are somewhere safe. Add the HP gain described above and 2 maximum SP. Neither a level gain nor a signature change refreshes spent Grit.

Your departure purse combines savings, community support, past work and class preparation.

Starting coins = 40 + ancestry + culture + background + class.

Add these once during character creation. This is a starting purse, not income each level. It does not use DP or attributes. Resolve card equipment grants before shopping; there is no coin reimbursement for a duplicate or declined grant.

Decide where these coins came from. Perhaps you saved your wages, received a gift from home or sold something precious to pay for the journey. The purse is what you carry on departure. Your family’s wealth and circumstances are yours to describe.

Restless, adaptable and fiercely invested in a life that never feels long enough.

Humans have no single stature, complexion or way of making a home. A short life beside the elder peoples can give an ordinary season an urgent importance: learn the trade, mend the friendship, see what lies beyond the ridge. Some make roots; others make roads between the places they love.

Adaptability takes many forms. One human gathers languages and acquaintances; another learns by failing until a stubborn problem yields. Neither ambition nor restlessness is compulsory. A human hero may want a quiet life enough to undertake a dangerous journey to protect it.

Rules

Short, dark-haired and quick; the next possibility is already tugging at your sleeve.

Wood Elves are shorter and more lightly built than High Elves, with dark hair, nimble limbs and expressive, angular faces. Similar ears and facial structures have given both peoples the name elf in other tongues. A Wood Elf watching a High Elf deliberate may wonder how anyone can bear to leave an interesting idea untried for so long.

Quick movement often accompanies quick feeling. Curiosity, anger and affection can arrive with equal force; many Wood Elves trust the first useful opening and discover its consequences afterward. Their rashness can become daring, and their impulsiveness can become generosity. Neither prevents a Wood Elf from learning patience or taking a promise seriously.

Their bodies lend themselves to balance and movement. Woodlands give those gifts abundant expression, but a Wood Elf raised among rooftops, ships or crowded streets remains a Wood Elf. Their community determines what those quick hands learn to do.

Tall, strong and deliberate; a long life leaves room to consider every word.

High Elves are tall and strongly built, with pointed ears and the fine, angular facial structure that leads outsiders to call them kin to Wood Elves. They are a different ancestry. Beside a compact, restless Wood Elf, a High Elf has the presence of a standing stone: upright, composed and difficult to hurry.

Their long lives encourage a broad view of consequences. Many listen through an argument before speaking, practice a movement until it wastes no effort, or remember a slight long after its author has forgotten it. Confidence can harden into arrogance, especially when patience is mistaken for superior judgment. Others learn that living a long time is no guarantee of being right.

A High Elf might be a laborer, a wanderer or a scholar. Strength and deliberation belong to their physical and temperamental inheritance; wealth, titles and courtly manners depend on the life they have led.

Broad shoulders, patient hands and a home made where mountain meets open sky.

Long ago, dwarven peoples took different roads. Some built their halls within mountains opening onto the surface world. Others traveled deeper into the earth. Centuries of separation, perhaps much longer, have left their descendants visibly different.

Hill Dwarves are the broad, stocky surface people: solid limbs, strong backs, dense hair and faces weathered by forge heat, mountain wind or ordinary years of work. Their halls connect stone interiors to roads, daylight and neighboring communities. Deep Dwarves are their distant kin, but a stranger would seldom mistake one for the other.

Endurance, craft and a lasting memory are familiar expressions of Hill Dwarf identity. A remembered debt may be a kindness worth returning as readily as an injury worth answering. A dwarf need not live in a mountain, work a forge or keep a grudge; the same steady body can belong to a sailor, gardener or traveling musician.

Grey skin, great watchful eyes and a quiet step beneath the weight of the world.

The ancestors of Deep Dwarves went farther down. Over long generations, the people of the depths became shorter and slighter than their surface cousins. Their skin ranges through shades of grey, and their large eyes gather the faint light of the underground. Narrow shoulders and economical movements suit passages where a broad surface dwarf would struggle.

Many are naturally shy. They watch before approaching, speak after listening and prefer a familiar companion to the attention of a crowded room. Reserve does not diminish curiosity, courage or conviction. A quiet Deep Dwarf may be the first to notice danger and the one who refuses to abandon a friend.

Stone, darkness and small changes in air or vibration shape their experience. Those raised above ground bring the same sensitive bodies to unfamiliar surroundings. No ancestral instinct supplies a map of tunnels they have never walked.

Ordinary footsteps and isolated impacts do not overwhelm this sense. You must touch the connected solid surface; moving targets share that surface, and attacks require their ordinary range and a clear path.

Ancestry: Deep Dwarf · Choice: one of your two traits · Action: Passive unless the description gives a time or action.

Quiet feet, a generous table and courage that surprises people who judge by height.

Halflings are small, compact people, larger than gnomes, with a gift for making limited space comfortable. Others often notice their height before noticing the person, a mistake a halfling may patiently correct or quietly put to use.

Hospitality and good company are familiar pleasures, but a generous table does not require an easy life. Courage can live beside trembling knees, a sharp tongue beside warm manners, and a taste for home beside an irresistible curiosity about the road. A halfling raised far from halfling communities brings their own customs to those possibilities.

Rules

Choose two of the five traits below. These are invitations to a familiar fantasy, not a required personality. Any ancestry may grow up in any culture.

  • @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.b39265b53fcf58e8]{Under Their Noses} — The grand folk rarely remember to look beneath the table.
  • @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.69c266abd0aebc93]{Quick Tongue} — You can talk your way through a negotiation, an argument or an accusation.

@UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.6819ea3497079763]{Ancestry choices}

Tiny fey bodies, long lives and minds forever asking what else a thing could become.

Gnomes are fey creatures, smaller even than halflings, with deft hands, keen senses and an intelligence that can make a complicated device seem almost embarrassingly obvious. Their faces carry the expressions of long experience, however easily a stranger mistakes their stature for youth.

Some say the gnomes left the world of fairie to explore possibilities its inhabitants had overlooked. Others insist they were thrown out, and disagree enthusiastically about what invention caused the trouble. Gnomes tell both stories. Whether anyone remembers the whole truth is another question.

Inventing and tinkering delight many gnomes: an unfamiliar mechanism invites examination, an accepted limitation invites an experiment. Others apply that same searching intelligence to music, medicine, argument or the behavior of friends. A gnome does not inherit a workshop or a profession. Their fey nature and extraordinary mind travel with them wherever they grow up.

Rules

Choose two of the five traits below. Temperamental tendencies are invitations, not a required personality. Any ancestry may grow up in any culture. Each chosen characteristic carries the benefits and side effects in its description.

  • @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.3c3832bbb69dae29]{Eyes from Elsewhere} — The painted door is convincing. Its shadow has forgotten where the sun is.

@UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.a378cabea7b674ac]{Ancestry choices}

Quick hands, shared effort and a future finally open to your own making.

Goblins are small, quick-bodied people with prominent ears and alert, expressive faces. For generations, orcs enslaved them, and outsiders learned to associate goblins with the cruelty of those who held them. Freedom did not immediately erase that reputation. It did give goblins the chance to build lives whose purpose was their own.

Many now seek a place through useful work, trade, exploration and the steady proof of being a reliable neighbor. Resourcefulness honed under deprivation can become skilled repair, careful husbandry or a gift for seeing value where others see rubbish. Cooperation can become friendship and enterprise rather than a necessity of survival.

A goblin adventurer may want to support a community, win recognition or simply discover what freedom feels like beyond familiar roads. Others were born free and have never seen an orc. Their ancestry carries a history; each goblin chooses what to make of the life ahead.

Rules

@UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.1c7652881c131039]{Ancestry choices}

Long limbs, great hands and a world whose doorways rarely give you room.

Tallfolk stand well above most neighboring peoples. Long arms, powerful frames and large hands make their scale evident even when they sit quietly. A borrowed chair, a crowded wagon or a low lintel can demand more thought than a heavy load.

Some enjoy the attention their height brings; others become practiced at folding themselves out of the way. Their bodies offer reach and leverage, but neither strength nor stature decides their character. A Tallfolk healer may work with extraordinary gentleness, while a shy scholar learns to endure being the first person everyone notices.

Their origins and communities belong to the campaign. They need no named giant ancestor or distant kingdom to take their place beside other adventurers. Choose how your hero lives at this scale, and which of its advantages they have learned to use.

Rules

  • @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.64d5a4e2c9d1a9c1]{Built for the Weather} — You pull your collar closed and keep pace through the driving sleet.

Made for a purpose. Set adrift before you learned what it was.

Oath-Bound are constructs brought into existence by an oath holder. Each was made for a higher purpose and carries a destiny, yet begins their life without knowing what that purpose or destiny is. They have been given existence without an explanation: a ship set adrift, with neither a chart nor a remembered destination.

Their oath holder is the source of that existence. An Oath-Bound may recognize a name, a presence or a sign of the one who made them. Calling upon that connection can bring conviction, understanding or strength. The answer may feel intimate even when the being who gives it remains a mystery.

Life among other peoples gives them relationships, work and ambitions of their own. A journey might uncover why they were made, or simply teach them what they value while searching. The character’s choices belong to the player; their hidden purpose offers a mystery to discover together with the Dungeon Architect.

Rules

Ancestry traits use the ordinary action, targeting and recovery procedures together with their printed grants.

Touch and object interactions

Ordinary physical reach extends to an adjacent square. A touch ability is one whose rules or narrative require contact with its target. An ability’s printed adjacency requirement describes distance; its description establishes whether it uses physical contact.

An explicit reach grant gives its printed distance for the interactions it names. Long Reach gives Tallfolk a range of 2 squares for object interactions and non-attack touch abilities. Use the ordinary action cost each time: picking up an object costs a Maneuver, and a touch ability spends its printed action and costs. Attack range follows the attack’s printed rules.

For example, a Tallfolk with Long Reach can pick up a key 2 squares away with a Maneuver, or use a healing touch ability on an ally 2 squares away. Each use follows its ordinary action cost.

Defense Boons when the attacker rolls

When the defender rolls, apply defense Boons and Banes to that defense roll. When a player-controlled attacker makes the roll instead, each applicable defense Boon becomes 1 Bane to the attack, and each applicable defense Bane becomes 1 Boon to the attack. Combine those with the attacker’s own Boons and Banes normally.

For example, Small Target gives a gnome 1 additional defense Boon against a ranged attack when the gnome already benefits from cover. Against an attack rolled by another player, that same covered ranged attack instead receives 1 Bane to the attacker’s roll.

Oath-Bound recovery

Oath-Bound count as living creatures for healing and use the ordinary hero rules for HP, scars, rest and recovery.

Paying HP costs

When an ability asks you to spend HP, pay its printed amount. This cost bypasses resistance and must leave you with at least 1 HP.

HP unavailable for recovery

When an ability makes spent HP unavailable for recovery until a stated time, record that HP and its release time. During that period, healing and overnight rest can restore HP up to maximum HP minus the unavailable amount. Record this separately from scars and maximum HP.

For example, an Oath-Bound with maximum HP 20 uses The Debt Comes Due and spends 1 HP. Until the next dawn, healing or overnight rest can restore them to 19 HP. At dawn, that HP becomes available for ordinary recovery again.

A reroll replaces the original roll for the same action or event. Use the original attribute and applicable Boons and Banes, roll again, and resolve the new result, including its retained natural dice.

Choose the people, places and experiences that shaped you. Choose two ancestry traits, a culture and a background. Any ancestry may come from any culture. An ancestry’s familiar temperament describes a tendency, never an obligation or an automatic attribute modifier.

Your ancestry supplies inherited traits. Culture describes a community and its traditions; background recalls something you did or experienced before adventuring. These choices offer connections, memories and capabilities. Only a trait’s printed rules grant mechanical benefits. Base-statistic changes are permanent; other benefits last while their stated circumstances apply.

Stature and space

For ancestry comparisons, Gnomes, Halflings and Goblins are Small; Humans, both Elves, both Dwarves, Tallfolk and Oath-Bound are Medium. Gnomes are physically smaller than halflings within the same category. Tallfolk remain Medium despite their height. A Large creature is one explicitly described as Large by its own entry. These labels provide the comparison used by Under Their Noses; they grant no automatic changes to damage, reach, Speed, Bulk capacity or equipment rules. Use physical description to decide whether a body can fit through an opening; an explicit trait may change the cost or difficulty of doing so.

Your other beginnings

Choose one culture and one background. Each offers two disciplines to study. Select one from each, then a third from your class, choosing three different disciplines. Spend your starting DP to learn the techniques and spells you want to practice.

You see who needs shelter and step into the space between them and harm.

The door shakes in its frame. Behind you, the apothecary is trying to get two frightened children out a window. You brace the latch with your shoulder and ask, very calmly, how much longer they need.

A Protector makes a company brave enough to take risks. You read a room for the person in danger and a battlefield for the ground you can actually hold. Step Between suits the guardian who stays within reach of their companions. Healing Hands carries that care past the moment of injury. An oathkeeper might choose Oathstrike and make an enemy answer for hurting someone they swore to defend.

You might take pleasure in a good watch roster, a repaired strap, or the moment someone trusts you enough to rest. What would make you lower your shield? Who taught you that asking for help can be part of keeping people safe?

Rules

Attributes: Minimum 0 in Fortitude, Reason. HP contribution: +3 at level 1 and per level thereafter.

Casting attribute: Reason.

You make the hard choices in the space between one stroke and the next.

When a duel spills out of the inn, everyone watches the swords. You notice the wet cobbles, the hitch in one fighter’s step, and the loose shutter that will block the archer’s view in a heartbeat. There is your opening.

A Blade is the company’s practiced weapon fighter. You shine when timing and position decide who can press the attack. One Blade rushes across open ground with Reckless Charge. Another waits behind Measured Guard. A third learns Cleave and goes looking for the moment two opponents stand too close. A bow and a patient eye can define a Blade just as readily as a rapier.

Perhaps you love sparring with someone who makes you change your habits, or hate the swagger of people who draw steel for an audience. Who put a weapon in your hand, and what did they teach you about when to leave it sheathed?

You study the impossible until your hands can give it a shape the world must briefly accept.

A thread of ash climbs the stair against the draft. You hold up a hand and the company stops. Someone has worked magic here. The ash is going to show you where they stood.

An Arcanist asks what a spell can do in this particular room, with these people in it. An elemental working might change the ground under a fight. A careful ritual might be the answer to a door the company would rather leave intact. Bent Trajectory lets an attack come from an unexpected angle. Study the Pattern suits a reader of workings, and Deliberate Spark is for the caster who sees an advantage in moving friends and foes a little farther apart.

You might savor a clean diagram or love the apprentice who asks the awkward question. What magical shortcut do you refuse to take? What impossible thing would make you put your notes down and try it anyway?

A Shepherd keeps people on their feet and helps them through trouble they cannot face alone. A punishing journey or a fight that leaves someone frightened and hurt gives you plenty to do. The wild lends you another shape without taking away your own life.

Rules

Once per scene, transform for 10 minutes into a familiar Small, Medium or Large ground beast, or a Small flying beast. Choose a legal space large enough for the form. Keep your HP, attributes, conditions, resources and Speed, and gain physical resistance 1. Your equipment melds and provides no effects or resistance. You speak only animal calls and cannot cast spells or use equipment. Return to your own shape with a Maneuver or automatically at 0 HP. Changing form never restores HP.

Spot the Leverage suits the investigator who looks for the detail that changes the plan. Make It Last can turn a plain lamp, tool, or shield into something the company will miss when it’s gone. You meet the obstacle with everything you are, and let it discover whether that is enough.

The barricade has started to give. You hear the beam crack and know there is time for exactly one decision. The others can follow through if you make a gap wide enough.

An Unbalanced brings force to the point where it will matter most. In a crowded fight you can break up the knot around a companion. At a contested passage you can give the company a way through before the chance passes. Go Berserk calls up the fury to stay in a fight. Charge suits the runner who sees a lane through the confusion. Grab and Hurl lets you turn a struggle over footing into an abrupt change of position.

You have never fit the expected answer, and have learned to make that useful.

A stranger at the ferry calls out in a language nobody in the company knows. You recognize the voice of the spirit at your shoulder. There is just enough time to decide whether to invite it in.

An Odd brings possibilities the company might never think to ask for. When the company reaches for a crowbar, you may be the one who asks whether the door has a name. Borrowed Tongue can turn a stranger’s warning into a conversation. Use Their Voice draws an enemy’s eye away from a companion. The Bargain suits an Odd whose power comes with a relationship worth playing out at the table.

You might collect the names of forgotten things, prefer a door with a story to one with a lock, or be the most practical person in a room full of omens. What makes the uncanny feel ordinary to you? What bargain would you walk away from, even if nobody understood why?

Rules

Action: Main Action · Attribute: None (no roll)

Target / range / shape: Self.

Your body falls prone and cannot act, move or take Reactions. It has 3 defense Banes. Your spirit appears in your square or an adjacent free square.

The spirit has Speed 5, can speak, can pass through nonmagical solid objects and creatures, and is not a legal target for ordinary attacks. It cannot attack, cast spells, use equipment or physically interact with objects. Its movement does not provoke opportunity attacks. Magical attacks can target it; resolve them against your normal defenses, and damage to the spirit is damage to your body. If your body drops to 0 HP, the projection ends.

At the end of your turn, choose one:

  • Snap Back: Your spirit returns to your body.
  • Manifest: Your body appears in the spirit’s square or the nearest free square that is not separated from your body by a solid barrier, prone. The projection ends.

If no legal Manifest square exists, you can only Snap Back.

Duration: Until the end of your turn.

Equipment / acquisition: A free hand for casting.

This is a spell costing 0 SP, usable once per scene. Attacks explicitly described as magical and spells may target the spirit; ordinary attacks target your body instead.

Duration: The scene.

Equipment / acquisition: A free hand for casting.

This is a spell costing 0 SP. Animals retain their motives and agency. A companion acquired through play uses its actual profile.

A shield bearer learns to turn a blow meant for a friend. A tracker reads where a fugitive left the road. A student of flame learns how to light a candle, then how to hold back pursuers with a wall of fire. What does your hero spend time practicing?

Begin with a discipline you already study or spend the DP your class lists to take up a new one. Choose an ability path or spellbook and learn its entries in order. Each entry tells you when you can learn it, what it costs, and what it lets you do. Save any DP you want to spend later.

Wear your protection as though it were part of you.

Wear armor you are trained to use to perform these techniques. Light Armor I teaches light armor, Light Armor III teaches medium armor, and Heavy Armor I teaches heavy armor at level 3. Each training supplies a compatible ordinary suit if you need one. A worn suit grants physical resistance 1 for light, 2 for medium, or 3 for heavy. Use the highest matching resistance. Damage reductions apply after resistance and respect the minimum for attacks; immunity remains an exception.

Advance

Armored Advance I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Main Action. Move up to your Speed along a legal route. Ignore the extra movement cost of the first square of nonmagical difficult terrain on this move. Gain Stability 1 until your next turn starts. No roll.

Armored Advance II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Armored Advance ignores the extra cost of the first two squares of nonmagical difficult terrain on this move.

Armored Advance III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Armored Advance grants Stability 2 instead of 1.

Ironbound Advance I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Main Action. Move up to your Speed, ignoring extra movement cost from nonmagical difficult terrain. Until your next turn starts, gain Stability 2 and reduce damage from attacks against you by 1 after resistance.

Ironbound Advance II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Ironbound Advance grants Stability 3.

Ironbound Advance III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Ironbound Advance reduces attack damage by 2 instead of 1.

The Unbroken Gate

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Main Action, with a held shield. Until your next turn starts, hold your position: you cannot move or be forcibly moved. Once during this stance, when an attacker chooses an adjacent ally as the sole target, you may become the target before the roll if you are a legal target. This interception costs no Reaction. During the stance, reduce attack damage against you by 3 after resistance. Once per scene, when you establish the stance, up to four willing allies within 3 squares may move 2 squares toward you without movement reactions.

Bracing

Brace I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Maneuver. While on solid footing, brace yourself to gain Stability 1 until your next turn starts. No roll.

Brace II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Brace grants Stability 2.

Brace III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 While Brace lasts, a push or pull that Stability reduces to 0 also fails to knock you Prone; its damage and other effects still apply.

Stand Like Stone I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Maneuver. Until your next turn starts, gain Stability 3 and cannot be moved against your will or knocked Prone while standing on a supporting surface. You cannot move voluntarily during this stance. No roll.

Stand Like Stone II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 While Stand Like Stone lasts, one willing adjacent ally also gains Stability 1 while adjacent.

Stand Like Stone III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Stand Like Stone can protect two willing adjacent allies, and gives each Stability 2 while adjacent.

Rooted against the Charge

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Maneuver. Brace a passage up to 3 squares wide while on solid footing. Until your next turn starts, you and up to three willing adjacent allies cannot be forcibly moved or knocked Prone while you remain stationary and they remain adjacent. Each protected creature reduces collision damage by 3 after resistance; this non-attack damage may reach 0. This does not prevent other damage or let creatures pass through blocked squares.

Deflection

Turn the Blow I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Reaction. After your defense roll, before physical damage from that attack is applied, reduce its physical damage by 1 after resistance. No roll.

Turn the Blow II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Turn the Blow reduces physical damage by 2.

Turn the Blow III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Turn the Blow reduces physical damage by 3.

Weather the Storm I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Reaction. After your defense roll, before damage from that attack is applied, reduce its damage by 2 after resistance. Until your next turn starts, also reduce physical damage from each later attack against you by 1 after resistance.

Weather the Storm II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Weather the Storm reduces the triggering attack’s damage by 3 instead of 2.

Weather the Storm III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Weather the Storm reduces later physical attack damage by 2 instead of 1.

Unyielding Shell

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Reaction. After your defense roll, before damage from that attack is applied, reduce its damage by 4 after resistance. Until your next turn starts, reduce damage from each further attack against you by 3 after resistance. Once per scene, this response also prevents new Bleeding and Dazed from the triggering attack; its other effects remain.

Harness

Light Armor I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Passive. You are trained to wear light armor; the suit supplies physical resistance 1. Ignore 1 Bulk from worn armor when calculating encumbrance, minimum 0 armor Bulk. This does not change its inventory size.

Light Armor II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 While wearing armor you are trained to use, gain 1 Boon on rolls to resist forced movement. This is not additional resistance or Stability.

Light Armor III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 You are also trained to wear medium armor; the suit supplies physical resistance 2. Your Speed increases by 1 while wearing armor you are trained to use.

Heavy Armor I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Passive. You are also trained to wear heavy armor; the suit supplies physical resistance 3. Maneuver: lift one willing or helpless adjacent creature no larger than you. For this turn, carrying it adds no encumbrance and occupies no weapon hand. Put it down in a legal adjacent square when your turn ends.

Heavy Armor II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 While wearing trained armor, ignore the extra cost of the first square of nonmagical difficult terrain you enter each turn. Heavy Armor’s carrying benefit lasts until the start of your next turn instead of turn end.

Heavy Armor III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Heavy Armor’s carrying Maneuver also lets you move 2 squares with the passenger without movement reactions. Place the passenger in a legal adjacent square when the carrying benefit ends.

Bring Everyone Home

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Main Action · Knowledge, wearing trained armor and holding a shield, with medical supplies. Once per scene, move up to 8 squares without movement reactions. Along the route treat up to three different willing or helpless creatures within reach: roll once; each with an available first-aid attempt restores 5/8/11 HP and spends that attempt. Carry one creature no larger than you along any part of the route without added encumbrance or using your shield hand; place it adjacent at the end. A spent allowance still permits rescue, not healing. Supplies must cover each treated patient.

Distance, timing and the practiced turn of a weapon.

Bladework, Impact and Dueling require a wielded melee weapon. Unarmed techniques use a free hand, foot or similar natural contact; a held weapon or shield is not an unarmed strike. Each attack uses its printed damage, rather than adding basic-attack damage. Improvements affect only their named technique. Movement requires a legal route; reactions to movement apply unless stated otherwise.

Bladework

Measured Cut I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Main Action · Brawn or Agility, chosen before rolling. Attack one adjacent creature for 2/3/5 physical damage. On Strong, you may move 1 square after the attack.

Measured Cut II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Measured Cut deals 3/4/6 physical damage.

Measured Cut III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Measured Cut also applies Bleeding 1 on Strong.

Sweeping Blade I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Main Action · Brawn. Attack up to three adjacent enemies. Roll once; each takes 1/2/4 physical damage. Each creature is struck once.

Sweeping Blade II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Sweeping Blade deals 2/3/5 physical damage to each target.

Sweeping Blade III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Sweeping Blade also pushes each target 1 square directly away on Strong. Resolve collisions normally.

Iron Tempest

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Main Action · Brawn. Move up to 3 squares, ignoring extra movement cost from difficult terrain, and attack up to three enemies adjacent at any point along that route. Roll once; each takes 3/5/8 physical damage. Each creature is struck once. Once per scene, you may instead strike four enemies for 4/7/10; after this sweep gain Stability 3 until your next turn starts.

Impact

Driving Opening I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Maneuver. Choose one visible creature. Before your turn ends, your next Main Action melee weapon attack against it pushes that creature directly away from your attack position, 1 square on Standard or 2 squares on Strong. Resolve collisions normally. Apply the push only to the chosen creature on that attack. Reusing this technique replaces its unused effect.

Driving Opening II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Driving Opening pushes 2 squares on Standard as well as Strong.

Driving Opening III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Driving Opening also applies Slowed 2 on Strong to that target. Before rolling the modified attack against a living creature with positive HP, you may declare it nonlethal: if its damage would reduce the target to 0 HP, leave it at 1 HP and make it Unconscious for 1 minute or until it next takes damage. It falls Prone.

Battering Stroke I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Maneuver. Prepare your next Main Action melee weapon attack against one chosen visible creature before this turn ends. That attack pushes the target 2 squares directly away on any result; resolve collisions normally. On Strong it also applies Dazed 1. This replaces Driving Opening on that attack.

Battering Stroke II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Battering Stroke also applies Slowed 2 on Strong. Its modified attack may use Driving Opening’s learned nonlethal declaration.

Battering Stroke III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Battering Stroke also sets the target’s movement to 0 until the end of its next turn on Strong. Forced movement still affects it.

Break the Encirclement

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Maneuver. Once per scene, move up to 4 squares, including a horizontal jump up to 3 squares to a visible landing, without movement reactions. Prepare Battering Stroke for your next Main Action melee weapon attack this turn. After that attack, up to two willing allies within 3 squares of you may each move 2 squares without movement reactions. This grants no attack itself.

Dueling

Blade Ward I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Reaction. After resolving your defense against a melee attack, before taking its damage, reduce that attack’s damage by 2 after resistance, respecting the attack minimum. No roll.

Blade Ward II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Blade Ward reduces damage by 3 instead of 2.

Blade Ward III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 After Blade Ward resolves, you may move 1 square without movement reactions.

Riposte I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Reaction · Brawn or Agility, chosen before rolling. After a melee attack against you resolves, attack its source if adjacent for 2/3/5 physical damage. You must survive and be able to act.

Riposte II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Riposte deals 3/4/6 physical damage.

Riposte III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 After Riposte, move 1 square without movement reactions; on Strong also apply Dazed 1 to its target.

Duelist’s Boundary

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Reaction · Brawn or Agility, chosen before rolling. When a visible adjacent enemy begins an attack against you or an ally, before its roll, strike it for 3/5/8 physical damage. On Standard or Strong it also gains Dazed 1. If it remains able to attack, resolve its attack normally; reduce its damage by 3 after resistance, respecting the attack minimum. This spends your ordinary Reaction and grants no further retaliation.

Unarmed

Empty-Hand Strike I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Main Action · Brawn or Agility, chosen before rolling. Strike one adjacent creature unarmed for 2/3/5 physical damage. Choose an available hand, foot or other natural contact; restraint that prevents that contact prevents the strike.

Empty-Hand Strike II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Empty-Hand Strike deals 3/4/6 physical damage.

Empty-Hand Strike III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Empty-Hand Strike also applies Slowed 1 on Strong. Before rolling against a living creature with positive HP, you may declare the strike nonlethal: if its damage would reduce the target to 0 HP, leave it at 1 HP, Prone and Unconscious for 1 minute or until it next takes damage.

Flowing Hands I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Main Action · Brawn or Agility. Move up to 2 squares without movement reactions and strike up to two different creatures adjacent at any point of the route. Roll once; each takes 1/2/4 physical damage. You may make each strike nonlethal using Empty-Hand Strike’s declaration before rolling.

Flowing Hands II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Flowing Hands deals 2/3/5 physical damage to each target.

Flowing Hands III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Flowing Hands also applies Dazed 1 and pushes each target 2 squares directly away on Strong; resolve collisions normally.

Empty-Hand Tempest

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Main Action · Brawn or Agility. Move up to 4 squares without movement reactions and strike up to three different adjacent creatures along that route. Roll once; each takes 3/5/7 physical damage, and on Strong becomes Prone. You may declare these strikes nonlethal before rolling. Once per scene, after the strikes, move up to 2 further squares without movement reactions.

Find a way where the easy road ends.

Climbing, swimming and jumping are ordinary actions. These techniques improve them, using real holds, breathable air, supports and available equipment. Choose a route with the holds, support and clear landing the movement needs.

Climbing

Sure Ascent I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Main Action. Climb up to 2 squares along a surface with usable holds, paying no movement. If danger requires a roll, use Brawn or Agility as appropriate with 1 Boon; a Weak result advances at least 1 square where passage is physically possible, with the DA’s stated complication. You also gain that Boon on ordinary climbing rolls.

Sure Ascent II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Sure Ascent lets you climb at 1 square per movement spent during ordinary movement. Its Main Action climbs up to 3 squares.

Sure Ascent III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 You may keep one hand free while stationary on a climb with usable holds. Sure Ascent’s Main Action climbs up to 4 squares.

A Line for Everyone I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Main Action, with rope and a secure anchor within reach. Rig a line up to 10 squares long. Up to six creatures may climb it at normal movement cost while secured. The rope must reach the route and does not bridge unsupported open space. No roll.

A Line for Everyone II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 A Line for Everyone can rig up to 15 squares of carried rope; creatures using it gain 1 Boon on climbing rolls for remaining hazards.

A Line for Everyone III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 A Line for Everyone can serve up to ten creatures. With secure anchors at both ends that you can physically reach, it can form a supported crossing over open space; it needs enough rope and supports for the load.

The Living Bridge

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Main Action. With a sound rope secured to an anchor you can reach, brace a crossing up to 20 squares long that you have physically established. Until you move, release it or become unable to act, up to eight willing creatures can each traverse the line at normal movement cost with 2 Boons on any required climbing or balance rolls. You may support a load totaling up to twice your normal carrying capacity; greater loads require additional supports. The route and anchor must bear that load.

Leaping

Running Vault I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Maneuver. After moving at least 2 squares this turn, jump up to 2 squares horizontally to a visible unoccupied landing. Spend no additional movement. Movement reactions apply.

Running Vault II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Running Vault reaches up to 3 squares.

Running Vault III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Running Vault ignores movement reactions during the jump.

Follow My Leap I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Maneuver. Use Running Vault and guide one willing adjacent ally through the same jump immediately after you. It lands adjacent to your destination; both landings must be legal.

Follow My Leap II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Follow My Leap reaches up to 4 squares horizontally.

Follow My Leap III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Follow My Leap can guide two willing adjacent allies through the jump, each to a different legal square adjacent to your destination.

Bounding Company

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Maneuver. Once per scene, after moving at least 2 squares, leap up to 5 squares horizontally and guide up to four willing allies initially within 2 squares through the same crossing. Each lands within 2 squares of your landing in a separate legal square. These jumps trigger no movement reactions. All travelers must be able to move; this grants no flight beyond the landing.

Balance

Catch Your Balance I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Reaction. When you would fall Prone and can move, remain standing instead. No roll.

Catch Your Balance II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Catch Your Balance can also catch a secure ledge within reach when you begin to fall, leaving you hanging instead. You need a free hand.

Catch Your Balance III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 After Catch Your Balance, you may move 1 square to a safe unoccupied surface within reach without movement reactions.

Catch Them Falling I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Reaction. Use a free hand to catch one adjacent falling creature no larger than you. From secure footing, bring it into a free adjacent square. You can instead hang together from a reachable hold that supports you both. No roll.

Catch Them Falling II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Before Catch Them Falling, move 1 square along a safe surface without movement reactions to reach the falling creature.

Catch Them Falling III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Catch Them Falling can catch a creature one Size larger than you when your footing and anchor support both creatures.

Defy the Fall

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Reaction. When a rope-linked group begins to fall, secure its rope to an anchor within reach or hold it yourself. Arrest the falls of up to four connected creatures whose combined weight the rope and anchor can bear; if holding it yourself, the load cannot exceed twice your normal carrying capacity. They hang from the rope and take no damage from this arrested fall. Spend a Main Action on each following turn to hold it yourself; releasing or losing the support resumes the fall. No roll.

Swimming

Strong Swimmer I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Passive. Gain 1 Boon on Brawn rolls to swim.

Strong Swimmer II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Strong Swimmer removes extra movement cost for swimming in calm water.

Strong Swimmer III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 You may tow one willing or helpless creature no larger than you without additional swimming movement cost.

Carry Them to Shore I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Main Action · Brawn. Swim up to 2/3/4 squares, towing one willing or helpless adjacent creature no larger than you. The current must permit passage; the passenger moves with you.

Carry Them to Shore II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Carry Them to Shore swims 3/4/5 squares.

Carry Them to Shore III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Carry Them to Shore can tow two willing or helpless adjacent creatures, each no larger than you, using a hand or sound tether for each.

Against the Flood

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Main Action · Brawn. Swim up to 4/6/8 squares through passable water, towing up to four willing or helpless creatures on sound tethers. Their combined load cannot exceed twice your carrying capacity. During this movement you and those passengers gain 2 Boons on rolls against the current or floating debris. This does not provide air or protection from unrelated attacks.

See the useful thing waiting inside the material.

Gather suitable tools and materials and find a place to work. Before rolling, agree with the DA on the finished project, its size, progress target and time per attempt. Make crafting attempts individually, counting each completed step once.

Repairs

Mend and Fit I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Main Action, with tools and a suitable brace or fastening: temporarily secure one damaged nonmagical item within reach so it can support its ordinary stationary load until your next turn ends. It gains no HP and cannot attack or protect from attacks while broken. Alternatively work for 10 minutes and roll Knowledge for 1/2/3 progress toward repairing an item that retains enough structure.

Mend and Fit II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Mend and Fit’s repair work adds 1/3/4 progress. Its temporary brace lasts 1 minute unless the item moves or receives further damage.

Mend and Fit III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Mend and Fit’s repair work takes 5 minutes per attempt.

Field Repair I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Main Action · Knowledge, with tools and materials. Work on a damaged nonmagical item within reach whose essential structure remains. Add 1/2/3 progress toward repairing it. Completion restores its ordinary function; HP restoration for an object with HP is set as part of the repair objective before work.

Field Repair II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Field Repair adds 1/3/4 progress.

Field Repair III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Field Repair gains 1 Boon when you can reach and work on all damaged components.

Make It Whole

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Main Action · Knowledge, with tools and matching replacement parts. Add 3/5/7 progress toward repairing one examined nonmagical mechanism or object within reach, including a shattered item whose essential pieces or replacements are available. The DA fixes the complete repair objective and restored HP before work. Completing it restores normal function, not magical properties or expended ammunition. Large structures still require access to every affected section.

Mixtures

Smoke in a Bottle I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Main Action · 1 hour · Knowledge, with alchemical tools and one purchased batch of smoke ingredients. Add 1/2/3 progress toward target 3 to prepare one smoke flask. Maneuver: throw a prepared flask to a visible point within 4 squares, consuming it. Smoke fills a 1-square-radius area until your next turn ends and blocks sight through it. No throwing roll.

Smoke in a Bottle II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Smoke in a Bottle flasks have throwing range 6 squares.

Smoke in a Bottle III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Smoke in a Bottle flasks last until the end of your second turn after throwing.

Screen the Retreat I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Maneuver. Throw two prepared Smoke in a Bottle flasks at separate visible points within their range. Consume both and resolve each normally.

Screen the Retreat II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Screen the Retreat may place its two flasks within 8 squares.

Screen the Retreat III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 After Screen the Retreat, you and one willing adjacent ally may each move 1 square without movement reactions from creatures whose sight of you is blocked by the smoke.

Screen the Company

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Maneuver. Throw up to three prepared smoke flasks at visible points within 8 squares, consuming each. Each cloud fills a 2-square radius until the end of your second turn after throwing. You and up to three willing allies within 3 squares may each move 2 squares afterward; creatures whose sight of a traveler is blocked by these clouds cannot make movement reactions against that movement. Smoke blocks allies’ sight as well. No roll.

Safeguards

Catch the Failure I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Reaction. When a visible component within reach begins to fail during a nonmagical task, use tools in hand to arrest it before the consequence resolves. Give the worker 1 Boon on the associated roll to prevent injury or material loss, if such a roll is possible. Once per distinct failure event; this does not improve the task’s progress roll or reverse damage already applied.

Catch the Failure II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Catch the Failure grants 2 Boons.

Catch the Failure III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Before Catch the Failure you may move 1 square along a safe route without movement reactions to reach the component.

Save the Work I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Reaction. When a visible component fails during a nonmagical project within reach, use a free hand and suitable tools to preserve one recoverable component or batch of ingredients from that failure. It grants no progress and does not prevent other consequences. Once per project between safe overnight rests; the DA identifies what can physically be caught or secured.

Save the Work II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Save the Work may preserve two recoverable components or batches from the same failure.

Save the Work III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Save the Work also grants the worker 2 Boons on its permitted roll against injury from that event, before that roll.

Prevent Catastrophe

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Reaction. Once per scene, when an observed nonmagical structure or mechanism within reach begins to collapse, jam or burst, use tools and a suitable support to hold it for one round before its failure resolves. It must be no larger than a doorway, wagon or 2-square section of a larger structure. Creatures have time to escape or repair it; unresolved failure occurs at the end of your next turn. Attacks, magic and continued damage resolve normally and can destroy the support sooner. No roll; the support must physically bear the load.

Workshop

Trail Workshop I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Passive. Learn two recipes from Bound Torches, Fletched Ammunition, Travel Food, Twisted Cord and Wooden Brace. With tools and ingredients, work at the recipe’s interval and roll Knowledge for 1/2/3 progress or inventory steps; its output cap applies. You may also build a brace, barricade or shelter with structural materials: 1 hour and Knowledge for 1/2/3 progress toward the DA’s construction objective.

Trail Workshop II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Trail Workshop teaches two more recipes from its list. Its construction work adds 1/3/4 progress.

Trail Workshop III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Trail Workshop adds 1/3/4 progress or inventory steps to its recipes, respecting output caps; construction attempts take 30 minutes.

A Roof before Nightfall I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Main Action · 1 hour, with tools and sound materials on stable ground. Build a weatherproof shelter for six people without a roll. It resists ordinary weather, not attacks or extreme hazards. You can also improvise a simple hook, wedge, lever or similar tool from suitable salvage: 10 minutes and Knowledge for 1/2/3 progress toward target 3. It lasts one task and cannot be a weapon, armor, consumable ingredient or valuable.

A Roof before Nightfall II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 A Roof before Nightfall accommodates eight people. Its improvised-tool work adds 1/3/4 progress.

A Roof before Nightfall III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 A Roof before Nightfall takes 30 minutes with materials already gathered, and you gain 1 Boon on subsequent repair rolls for that shelter.

A City Opens Its Gates

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Main Action · 1 day · Reason. Present a feasible civic project to representatives of up to four willing factions you can communicate with. Show how it would work with a plan, model or demonstration. Roll once; add 4/7/10 progress to each faction’s separate agreement objective. Completion secures the commitments established by the DA, such as access, labor or a ceasefire. New terms need a new objective; this creates neither resources nor control over a settlement.

Find the distance where a deliberate step matters more than a heavy swing.

Fencing requires a one-handed melee weapon suited to precise cuts or thrusts, such as a saber, shortsword or rapier, wielded in one hand. Each attack uses its printed damage. Follow the usual movement reactions unless the technique says otherwise.

Pointwork

Direct Thrust I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Main Action · Agility. Attack one adjacent creature for 1/2/4 physical damage. On Standard or Strong, you may move 1 square after the attack without triggering movement reactions.

Direct Thrust II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Direct Thrust deals 2/3/5 physical damage.

Direct Thrust III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 After a Strong Direct Thrust, you may move up to 2 squares instead of 1, avoiding movement reactions.

Broken Tempo I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Main Action · Agility. Move up to 2 squares, then attack one adjacent creature for 2/3/5 physical damage. Neither this approach nor a 1-square step you may take immediately after the attack triggers movement reactions.

Broken Tempo II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Broken Tempo deals 2/4/6 physical damage.

Broken Tempo III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 On Strong, Broken Tempo also applies Dazed 1 to the target.

The Unseen Line

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Main Action · Agility. Move up to 4 squares and attack one enemy adjacent at any point along your route for 2/4/7 physical damage. On Strong, apply Dazed 1 and Bleeding 1. You may continue the route after the attack. This movement avoids movement reactions.

Footwork

Passing Step I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Maneuver. Move 1 square without triggering movement reactions. No roll.

Passing Step II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Passing Step lets you move up to 2 squares instead of 1.

Passing Step III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 One square of Passing Step may cross a square occupied by a willing ally. You must end in a legal unoccupied square.

Outside Measure I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Maneuver. Move up to 3 squares without triggering movement reactions. If you end adjacent to any enemy you were not adjacent to when you began this Maneuver, choose one of them. Gain 1 Boon on your next melee weapon attack against it this turn. No roll.

Outside Measure II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 One square of Outside Measure may cross a square occupied by a willing ally. You must end in a legal unoccupied square.

Outside Measure III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Outside Measure lets you move up to 4 squares.

Needle Through the Press

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Maneuver. Once per scene, move up to 5 squares without triggering movement reactions, ignoring extra movement cost from difficult terrain. You may pass through occupied squares and must end in a legal unoccupied square. Choose one enemy you passed adjacent to. Gain 2 Boons on your next melee weapon attack against that enemy this turn. This replaces any unused Boons from Outside Measure. No roll.

Blade Contact

Deflecting Parry I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Reaction. Before you roll defense against an adjacent enemy’s melee weapon attack, add 1 Boon to that defense. No separate roll.

Deflecting Parry II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 On a Strong defense, Deflecting Parry lets you move 1 square after the attack without triggering movement reactions.

Deflecting Parry III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Deflecting Parry works against melee attacks from adjacent enemies using weapons, natural attacks or unarmed strikes.

Answering Steel I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Reaction · Agility. After an adjacent enemy finishes a melee attack against you, strike it for 1/2/4 physical damage if your defense was Standard or Strong and it remains adjacent.

Answering Steel II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Answering Steel deals 2/3/5 physical damage.

Answering Steel III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 After a Strong Answering Steel counterattack, you may move 1 square without triggering movement reactions.

Counter in Tempo

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Reaction · Agility. When an adjacent enemy finishes a melee attack against you or an adjacent ally and the defense was Standard or Strong, attack it for 2/4/7 physical damage. On Strong it gains Dazed 1. After your counter, you may move up to 2 squares without triggering movement reactions. You must be able to act and the enemy must still be adjacent.

Blade Tricks

Bind the Blade I

DP: 1 | Level: 1 Main Action · Agility. Attack an adjacent enemy wielding a melee weapon for 1/2/3 physical damage. On Standard or Strong, that weapon’s next attack takes 1 Bane if made before your next turn starts.

Bind the Blade II

DP: 2 | Level: 1 On Strong, Bind the Blade imposes 2 Banes instead of 1.

Bind the Blade III

DP: 2 | Level: 1 Bind the Blade deals 1/3/4 physical damage.

Strip the Grip I

DP: 3 | Level: 3 Main Action · Agility. Attack an adjacent enemy holding a weapon for 1/3/4 physical damage. On Standard or Strong, choose one of its held weapons. It drops that weapon in its square if it can release it. If it cannot release the weapon, its next attack with it before your next turn starts takes 1 Bane.

Strip the Grip II

DP: 4 | Level: 3 Strip the Grip imposes 2 Banes instead of 1 when you choose a weapon the target cannot release.

Strip the Grip III

DP: 4 | Level: 3 You may move the weapon Strip the Grip dislodges into a legal unoccupied square adjacent to the target instead.

Surrender the Steel

DP: 5 | Level: 7 Main Action · Agility. Once per scene, attack an adjacent enemy holding a weapon for 2/4/6 physical damage. On Standard or Strong it drops one held weapon of your choice if it can release it. Move the dropped weapon up to 2 squares along a clear route to an unoccupied square. On Strong, you may instead guide it up to 2 squares along a clear route into your free hand. On Standard or Strong, if the target cannot release the weapon, it takes 2 Banes on its next attack with that weapon before your next turn starts.
