A drawn blade changes the conversation. A broken bridge changes the journey. The rules help you decide what those changes mean when timing, danger and the choices of several characters meet.

Begin with what your hero is doing. You can use a learned ability, take a universal action, or describe something the situation makes possible. The DA establishes the circumstances and calls for a roll only when uncertainty has consequences.

Resolve an action

When you use an ability, declare it before rolling. Read its requirements, choose its targets and any printed options, and check range and equipment. Spend the action and any required cost. Roll its attribute if instructed, then apply the complete Weak, Standard or Strong outcome. Finally, record conditions and continuing effects.

An outcome is complete: do not add the Weak damage to the Standard damage. If a Strong outcome includes an earlier benefit, it says so. Instant damage happens once; a condition applied by that damage follows the condition's own timing.

Spend the printed action even when an ability needs no roll. If the action lists a time, finish the full time before resolving it. Wild Harvest is a Main Action that takes 1 hour. A Ritual uses its full casting time. When an ability lists another use or a triggered Reaction, follow the timing for that use.

Boons, Banes and results

Roll three dice, plus one die for each net Boon or Bane, to a maximum of six dice. With Boons, retain the best three; with Banes, retain the worst three. Add the printed attribute once. Weak is 8 or less, Standard 9–14, and Strong 15 or more.

CircumstanceUsual adjustment
Meaningful help or obstacle1 Boon or Bane
Substantial help or a severe obstacle2 Boons or Banes
Exceptional advantage or difficulty, still possible3 Boons or Banes

These are guides for the DA. They do not turn an impossible attempt into a possible one. Do not count the same obstacle twice under different names. Boons and Banes from distinct valid sources stack, cancel, and then use the three-die net limit.

> Example — keeping the best three. An attack has 3 Boons and 1 Bane, leaving > 2 Boons. Roll five dice. On 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, retain 4, 5, 6 for 15. Brawn +1 makes > 16, a Strong result. If two Banes remained instead, retain 1, 2, 4 for 7; Brawn +1 > would give 8, a Weak result. Neither roll changes the attack's printed damage.

Read retained natural 111 as Weak with an additional complication and 666 as Strong with an additional benefit. The result still makes its printed progress. The DA fits a benefit or complication to the scene; it does not silently double damage or grant another action. Death rolls use only the result band.

Taking turns

A round lasts 6 seconds, so 10 rounds make 1 minute. Each character takes one turn during that time.

At the start of combat, the DA decides whether either side has pulled off an ambush. If so, the ambushing side starts without an initiative roll. Otherwise, one player rolls unmodified 3d6. On 12 or more, the players start. On 11 or less, the opposition starts. The starting side opens every round of this combat.

An ambush comes from the setup, such as catching opponents unaware from cover. Declaring an attack first leaves the usual initiative procedure in place. Both sides take their usual turns in the first round. Use the ordinary rules for concealment, cover and positioning.

The starting side chooses one of its characters to act. Then the other side chooses one. Alternate until everyone has taken a turn. If one side has no characters left to act, the other finishes its remaining turns. Each side chooses its order as it goes.

On your turn, you have one Main Action, one Maneuver, and movement up to your Speed. You also have one Reaction, available for its stated trigger. Refresh that turn's budget at the start of your turn. A defense roll does not itself spend a Reaction. Choose your retained categories at turn start if Dazed or Grappled.

You can split movement around your actions. You can convert your Main Action into a Maneuver and a Maneuver into another movement allowance. Conversion goes only in that direction. Converting your Main and original Maneuver into movement gives three total movement allowances: a full sprint.

> Example — reaching an ally. Speed 6 lets Mara move 6 squares. She converts her > Maneuver into movement for 6 more, then uses her Main Action to heal a companion. > She has not gained a second Main Action, and any difficult terrain costs still apply.

A Reaction resolves when its trigger says it does, including on someone else's turn. Once spent, it is unavailable until refreshed. A free attack granted by an ability spends no action and may occur more than once in a turn, but free attacks never trigger additional free attacks. Read the granting effect to see which attack it allows.

Attacking and defending

Players roll. When your hero attacks, roll the attack's printed attribute and read its attacker outcomes. This is true even if the target is another player character; the receiving player does not also roll a defense.

When a DA-controlled creature attacks you, roll the defense attribute specified by that attack. It might be Agility to evade a blow, Fortitude to withstand a bodily assault, or another attribute named by the attack. Apply the result from its Weak defense / Standard defense / Strong defense columns. Weak defense is the most dangerous outcome; Strong defense is the least dangerous.

Player's defenseEquivalent attacker outcome
WeakStrong attack
StandardStandard attack
StrongWeak attack

Creature Evasion adds its printed Boons or Banes to your attack. Threat adds its printed Boons or Banes to your defense against that creature's attack. These use the ordinary dice rules; do not add them numerically to the total.

If you control a summon, roll that creature's printed attributes. Its player profile already presents attack outcomes in the correct direction. Your hero's own Brawn or Reason does not replace the summon’s value.

For NPC-only actions, a player or the DA assuming the player role rolls. For an NPC attack against another NPC, roll the defender’s printed attribute and read the attacker’s defense-outcome table. For consequential healing or another task, roll the acting NPC’s attribute. Make one roll; handling dice does not transfer control of the NPC. Off-screen events can use DA judgment.

Damage and resistance

Damage comes from the chosen outcome, not a weapon damage die. Your attribute has already affected the roll; do not add it again to damage. Apply each matching resistance after determining the outcome. Armor DR is physical resistance.

Use the highest applicable resistance of each type, to a maximum of 3. Two sources of physical resistance 2 do not give 4. Physical resistance 2 and Fire resistance 1 can apply together because they protect against different types.

An attack that deals damage has a minimum of 1 total damage after reductions if any of its original damage survives immunity. Damage from conditions, falls, and collisions can be reduced to 0.

> Example — steel and flame. An attack deals 3 physical and 1 fire damage. > Physical resistance 2 reduces the physical portion to 1. Fire resistance 1 removes > the fire portion. Take 1 total damage, not one of each type. If both portions had > been reduced to zero by resistance, the attack would still deal 1 total damage.

Physical includes impacts, sonic force and supernatural force when the attack says physical. Fire, Cold and Lightning have separate resistances. Life resistance reduces magical healing and potions. First Aid and rest ignore Life resistance.

Damage and condition immunities

Use the immunities listed for the creature or granted by an effect. Damage immunity removes the named damage type from the event before weakness or resistance. If immunity removes all of the damage, the event deals 0 HP damage. The rest of the outcome still applies unless its rules require damage or prevent the effect. Condition immunity prevents the named condition from applying.

Damage immunities can name Physical, Fire, Cold, Lightning, Poison, Life, Radiant, Mental, or Force. Condition immunities name a specific condition. The bestiary includes immunity to Asleep, Bleeding, Blinded, Frightened, and Poisoned. A creature or effect can explicitly name another condition.

Against Fire damage immunity, a hit for 2 Physical and 3 Fire loses its Fire damage. If Physical resistance reduces the remaining damage to 0, the hit still deals 1 total damage.

> Example — Burning 2. Fire resistance 3 reduces the tick to 0 damage, as > does Fire damage immunity. In both cases Burning drops to 1 at turn end. > A creature immune to Burning never gains the condition, and a separate Fire > hit can still damage it.

Same-kind numerical bonuses do not add together unless explicitly stated. Conditions with meaningful ratings can add; binary Prone cannot. Boons and Banes use their own stacking rules. Weakness X adds X to its matching damage component before resistance, once per event. Use the highest value of each type, normally capped at 3. It cannot add a damage type absent from the attack. Special vulnerabilities use their printed procedure. Fire Weakness 2 turns 3 fire damage into 5 before resistance; it adds nothing to a purely physical attack.

Shields and guarded positions

Defend is a universal Maneuver that gives 1 Boon to defenses until the start of your next turn. Repeating Defend does not increase that same benefit.

When the DA judges your held shield can block an attack against you, spend your Reaction before the roll to Shield Block. While holding the shield, gain 1 Boon to defenses against blockable attacks until the start of your next turn. If the attacker rolls instead, apply 1 Bane to the attack roll. Most ordinary physical attacks can be blocked. Combine Defend and Shield Block as separate sources.

Opportunity attacks

Leaving an enemy's melee reach voluntarily, including by crawling, can provoke. Casting beside an enemy, standing, stowing an item, or retrieving one can also provoke. Spend your Reaction to make Basic Melee with a held melee weapon or Basic Unarmed with a free hand. A DA creature uses its bestiary Basic Melee. Resolve the attack at the start of the provoking action, before the original action takes effect.

Then continue the original action if its actor is capable. Damage alone does not cancel it. Recheck targets and range before continuing. At 0 HP, an actor must regain HP before they can act again. Commit the action on declaration; if interrupted permanently, that action is spent. Pay the printed cost when the action continues into resolution. An unspent potion is not drunk by an interrupted character who can no longer act.

Drawing a weapon as part of attacking adds no separate action. Dropping an item is free. Stowing or picking up an item costs a Maneuver. Forced movement never provokes. An ability can explicitly allow movement without provoking.

> Example — a spell under pressure. Vaelis begins casting beside an armed foe. > The foe spends its Reaction on Basic Melee. Vaelis makes the required defense and > loses HP. Vaelis can still act, so she checks her targets again, pays the > spell's SP cost and resolves it. If the attack drops her to 0 HP, she spends > the action she declared and keeps the SP.

Distance, space and cover

All distances use squares. A square is the useful unit for your map; it does not require a fixed conversion into feet or meters. Normal ground costs 1 movement per square and difficult ground costs 2. While Prone, crawl for 2 movement per normal square or 3 per difficult square. Straight and diagonal steps cost the same. Standing costs 2 movement.

You can cross an occupied square if its occupant is Prone. Pay the higher of 2 movement or your usual cost to enter it, and finish in a free square. An ability that moves you without provoking still respects terrain, occupied spaces and legal endpoints unless it explicitly says otherwise.

Count the squares to your target or the point where you place a spell.

RangeSquaresCommon uses
Touch1Melee attacks and touch spells
Short6Thrown weapons and nearby spells
Long12Ordinary ranged weapons and long-range spells
Extreme18Spells such as Meteor Swarm

When an attack uses your weapon’s range, you can reach one band farther. A thrown weapon can reach a target 7–12 squares away and an ordinary ranged weapon can reach one 13–18 squares away. Take 1 Bane on that attack, or give the target 1 Boon if they roll defense. Beyond the extra band the target is out of range. Use the distance given for a spell or a technique with its own reach or trigger. A spell’s area extends according to its shape from the point you choose within range.

A sight-required target must be visible to you or located by an explicit alternative-sense targeting grant. An attack needs a usable path to its target. The DA judges whether an obstruction protects the target from that attack. Partial cover gives the attacker 1 Bane. Heavy cover gives the attacker 3 Banes and still leaves a narrow attack path, as through a thicket. If you roll defense, take 1 Boon for partial cover or 3 Boons for heavy cover instead. Apply cover once, using the usual Boon and Bane rules. A barrier that blocks the path prevents the attack.

For a player area attack, choose the printed range, shape, inclusion and exclusions. Roll once using the worst applicable net Boon/Bane situation among its targets. Use that result for all targets; apply their resistances individually. When an NPC area attack affects several players, each player makes their own defense roll.

Forced movement

  • Push X moves the target up to X squares directly away from the source.
  • Pull X moves the target up to X squares directly toward the source.
  • Slide X moves the target up to X squares in any direction, including vertically.

If you use the effect, choose the Slide path or where to stop a Push or Pull. Follow any restrictions printed in the effect. A Push or Pull changes elevation only if its effect allows it. A creature thrown by an ability follows that ability's directions. You can stop before using the full distance. Collision damage occurs only if the target actually hits something.

Apply Stability once to the initial target, reducing the available forced movement to a minimum of 0. Stability is normally 0. Use the highest explicit grant, to a maximum of 3.

Spend the entered square's terrain cost from the movement budget. If any positive budget remains, the target enters the final square even if its cost exceeds that budget, then stops. For example, push 1 can enter one difficult square and stop. Stability does not reduce Prone, conditions, voluntary movement, projectile range, obstacle progress or the reduction of a grapple.

When a moving creature hits a movable creature or object, they move together on what remains of the original movement allowance. On each new impact, everyone in the group and whatever it strikes take physical damage equal to the movement remaining at contact. Creatures and objects with HP each apply their own damage defenses. For an object without HP, the DA decides how the impact affects it. A movable object that breaks drops out of the group. Resolve damage before subtracting a new creature's Stability, once per creature for that movement. Continued contact deals no further damage.

A fixed barrier stops the group even if it breaks. Add 1 to the damage dealt to each group member and the barrier before resistance. After placing the group, only the original mover bounces one square opposite the impact. If that square is blocked, the mover stays in place without another collision or damage.

> Example — A third creature joins. Two creatures moving together hit a third > with 3 squares left. Each takes 3 damage before armor. The new creature has > Stability 2, so the whole group has 1 square left to move.

> Crowded collisions. Moving groups must finish in separate legal spaces. > If everyone cannot fit, stop at the last position where they can; the DA decides > the arrangement. Placement cannot pass through walls or grant extra forward > movement.

Grappling and capture

Grappling requires a learned ability; it is not automatically granted with Basic Melee. Grappled prevents movement. At ratings 1, 2 and 3, retain respectively two, one or none of Main Action, Maneuver and Reaction, chosen at turn start. The grappler is restricted by their own contribution as well. Multiple grapplers' contributions add on the target. Attacks against a Grappled target gain Boons equal to its rating.

If you still have a Main Action, Force can reduce your grapple by 1/2/3. At Grappled 3 or higher, you can escape only if a grappler releases you or an outside intervention breaks the hold. For example, an ally can move the grappler out of reach or knock them unconscious. A grappler can freely release their own contribution. A maintained grapple lasts until the hold ends.

Attacks are lethal by default. An ability such as Pinning Strike can give you a nonlethal option. Declare that option before rolling and follow the ability's printed outcome. You can also take someone alive by securing their surrender, making them helpless, or holding them with a grapple.

With a free hand and suitable @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.da003d91ba817502]{restraints}, spend a Maneuver to cuff an adjacent creature that has surrendered, is helpless, or is Grappled 3 or higher. Once it is cuffed, a grappler can release their hold. The restraints bind the limbs they enclose until opened or escaped. Return to ordinary narration when the captive is secured and the immediate fight is over.

> An ally has knocked a guard unconscious with a nonlethal Pinning Strike. You > move beside the guard and spend a Maneuver to cuff their wrists. When the guard > wakes, the cuffs still bind their hands.

Ending a fight

A fight ends when the immediate opposition is resolved, not because everyone decides to ignore an active death roll. Resolve Dying before leaving combat timing. When it is safe to pause and companions can attend to an ordinary fire or similar immediate hazard, settle that hazard as the scene allows. Other conditions remain until their own removal, expiry or remedy. Safe overnight rest restores HP and SP; it does not erase scars, refund Grit, cure every condition or restore the dead. A brief pause gives no recovery.

Light and perception determine what a hero can observe and target. An ability grants the sense, rating or range it names; use the shared definitions here to resolve it.

Light and sight

In complete darkness, no one can see.

In low light, the Dungeon Architect assigns 1 to 3 Banes according to the level of darkness. Apply these Banes to observation attempts and actions that require vision.

IlluminationSight-related Banes
Clear light0
Dim light1
Very dim light2
Barely perceptible light3

The table gives guidance for describing a lighting penalty. Judge the light reaching the subject of the attempt and apply that penalty once to the roll. Other sources of Boons and Banes use the ordinary resolution rules.

Low-Light Vision

Low-Light Vision has a rating. Ignore that many Banes imposed by low light, to a minimum of zero low-light Banes. Remove the ignored lighting Banes before combining the roll’s remaining Boons and Banes.

For example, in light imposing 3 Banes, Low-Light Vision 1 leaves 2 low-light Banes. Low-Light Vision 2 leaves 1. In complete darkness, no one can see.

Seismic Vision

While touching a continuous solid surface, Seismic Vision lets you pinpoint moving creatures and objects touching that surface within the sense’s printed range. It works in complete darkness.

You may use this perception to target a creature or object it locates. Use the attack’s or ability’s ordinary range and require a clear path to the target.

For example, a Deep Dwarf with The Stone Tells You can pinpoint a creature moving across the same connected stone floor within 6 squares, even after the lantern goes out. They can target that creature with an ability whose range and clear path reach it.

Other forms of perception

Sonar, seismic, thermal and spiritual perception are distinct forms of perception. A named sense uses its own means of gathering information. Its rules state what it perceives and how that information supports observation and targeting; its granting ability supplies any printed range.

These summarize the approved system. Bruce resolves discrepancies; current cards and rules are the source, not earlier editions.

Resolution

Roll only for uncertainty with consequences. Correct fictional action may reveal a clue without a roll. The DA asks for Brawn, Fortitude, Agility, Guile, Knowledge or Reason; the player takes an action which may call for that roll. Force is an action, not another attribute or a separate skill-roll category.

Roll 3d6 plus one attribute. Weak is 8 or below: progress, not automatic success. Standard is 9–14. Strong is 15 or above. Three natural retained sixes give Strong plus a benefit; three retained ones give Weak plus a complication.

Boons and Banes cancel. Use at most three net extra dice, retaining the best or worst three. Difficulty comes through Banes, never another target number on the same roll. A cumulative task’s progress target is a different thing: 1/2/3 progress per Weak/Standard/Strong result.

Turns and attacks

At combat start, the DA decides whether either side has pulled off an ambush. An ambushing side starts without an initiative roll. Otherwise, one player rolls unmodified 3d6. On 12 or more, the players start. On 11 or less, the opposition starts. The starting side opens every round.

Alternate sides from the first turn of combat. Each side chooses its next character, and the side with turns remaining finishes them when the other runs out. A round lasts 6 seconds and ends after everyone has had a turn. Each character has Main, Maneuver, Reaction and movement. Main converts to Maneuver, and Maneuver converts to movement. Conversion goes in that direction only.

When an ability gives a time with its action, complete the full time before resolving it. Wild Harvest takes 1 hour. A Ritual is a Main Action and uses its full casting time. Each separate use or triggered response follows its own timing.

Player attacks use one attacker roll, even against a player. NPC attacks use the player’s defense roll. Strong defense receives Weak attack effects, Standard receives Standard, Weak receives Strong. The defense itself spends no Reaction. Players roll their controlled creatures’ printed attack and defense attributes. For NPC-only actions, either a player or the DA assuming the player role rolls. For an NPC-versus-NPC attack, roll the defender’s printed defense attribute and read the attacker’s defense-outcome table. For consequential NPC healing or other tasks, roll the acting NPC’s printed attribute and outcomes. Apply the ordinary modifiers and use one roll; handling the dice does not transfer control of the NPC. Off-screen events may be resolved by DA judgment without simulating combat.

Damage is fixed by the card. Remove components covered by damage immunity first. Apply weakness, then the highest resistance of each remaining type, normally capped at 3, then other reductions. An attack deals a minimum of 1 total damage if at least one positive damage component survived immunity. Damage outside the attack's immediate outcome, such as condition ticks, falls, and collisions, can be reduced to 0. A fully immune event deals 0 HP damage. Conditions and other riders follow their own rules. Condition immunity prevents the named condition from applying. Use the explicit immunities on the creature or granted by an effect.

Damage types are Physical, Fire, Cold, Lightning, Poison, Life, Radiant, Mental, and Force. Current bestiary condition immunities are Asleep, Bleeding, Blinded, Frightened, and Poisoned. A creature or effect can explicitly name another condition.

Numerical weakness — approved October 16, 2026: Weakness X increases the matching damage component by X before resistance. Apply each weakness once per damaging event. Use the highest applicable weakness of each type, not the sum of multiple sources, with a normal cap of 3. A damaging effect must include that type; weakness does not add an absent damage type.

Example: Fire Weakness 2 changes 3 fire damage to 5 before resistance. An event dealing 4 physical and 1 fire instead becomes 4 physical and 3 fire; an event dealing only 4 physical is unchanged. Apply matching resistances next.

Special vulnerabilities, such as fire stopping regeneration, use their printed procedure. They do not imply numerical weakness or extra damage unless stated.

Attack range

Measure range in squares. Touch and ordinary melee reach 1 square. Short range is 6 squares, long range is 12, and extreme range is 18. A spell uses its listed range. Measure the reach to the spell’s target or chosen point, then apply its printed shape and area separately.

Thrown weapons have short range and ordinary ranged weapons have long range. An attack that uses the weapon’s range can reach one band farther. Apply 1 Bane to the attack roll or 1 Boon to the defense roll. Beyond that extra band the target is out of range. Combine this modifier with cover or other circumstances using the usual Boon and Bane rules. A technique’s explicit reach or trigger distance uses the number it gives.

Cover

The DA judges whether an obstruction protects the target from the attack. Partial cover gives the attacker 1 Bane. Heavy cover leaves a narrow attack path and gives the attacker 3 Banes. If the defender rolls, apply the same number as Boons on that defense roll. Apply cover once to the roll being made, using the usual Boon and Bane rules.

An attack needs a usable path. A barrier that blocks the path prevents the attack. An attack that requires sight needs a visible target or an explicit alternative that permits targeting. Follow the attack's printed targeting rules.

Movement

Entering a normal square costs 1 movement and entering a difficult square costs 2. While Prone, crawl for 2 movement per normal square or 3 per difficult square. Use the same costs for straight and diagonal steps. Standing costs 2 movement. You may cross an occupied square if its occupant is Prone. Pay the higher of 2 movement or your usual cost to enter it, and finish in a free square. Crawling is voluntary movement and can provoke when you leave an enemy’s melee reach. Forced movement consumes the entered terrain’s cost. Any positive remaining budget can enter the final square and stop even if that cost exceeds the budget.

Push X moves the target up to X squares directly away from the source. Pull X moves it up to X squares directly toward the source. Slide X moves it up to X squares in any direction, including vertically. The effect’s user chooses the path for a Slide and can stop any of these movements early. A Push or Pull changes elevation only if its effect allows it. Follow any restrictions in the effect. Collision damage requires an actual impact.

Collisions gather movable creatures and intact movable objects into a group that moves as one creature on the original remaining allowance. Each new impact deals physical damage equal to the movement remaining at contact to every member of the group and whatever it strikes. Creatures and objects with HP each apply their own damage defenses. The DA judges the impact on objects without HP. Remove any movable object that breaks, including one reduced to 0 HP. Then deduct a newly struck creature’s Stability once for that movement. Continued contact between group members deals no further damage.

A fixed barrier stops the group even if it breaks. Add 1 to the damage dealt to each group member and the barrier before resistance. After placement, only the original mover bounces one square opposite the impact. If that square is blocked, the mover stays in place without another collision or damage.

Group placement — approved October 16, 2026: move the group along the forced movement path and finish in separate legal spaces. If everyone cannot fit, stop at the last position where they can. The DA determines the exact arrangement; placement cannot pass through walls or grant extra forward movement.

All actors have @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.3292b6a49dcf7236]{Stability}: default 0, explicit grants only, maximum 3, highest source. It consumes forced movement once per newly struck creature, including through a collision chain; no protection against Prone or conditions.

Conditions

Resolve a temporary numbered condition at turn end, then reduce by 1. Burning and Freezing deal their rating in matching elemental damage; Bleeding bypasses resistance. Poisoned applies its rating in Banes, not damage. Frightened supplies Banes while the stated source is perceptible. Slowed reduces Speed.

Dazed 1/2/3 leaves two/one/no categories among Main, Maneuver and Reaction; choose at turn start. Movement remains. Paralyzed stops actions and movement at any positive rating; its number is duration. Blinded and Deafened numbers are duration, not severity. An asterisk prevents automatic decay; a persistent binary sense loss needs only rating 1*. Removal follows the source.

Grappled prevents movement and reduces action choices like Dazed; it is maintained, not decaying. The grappler suffers their own contribution too. Force can reduce Grappled while Main is retained. At rating 3 or higher, escape requires a grappler’s release or an outside intervention that breaks the hold. Separation beyond reach, unconsciousness, or death ends that grappler’s contribution. Attacks gain Boons equal to the actual target’s Grappled rating. Greater restriction applies when combined with Dazed, not their sum. Prone is binary. Hidden is universal, not observer-by-observer.

A mixed permanent/temporary bookkeeping rule is recorded in the full condition reference. Do not let a new temporary effect become permanent merely because another is starred.

Summons, exploration and recovery

Summoned forms — approved October 16, 2026: summons are shaped from energies to resemble and act like their creatures, not actual physical creatures brought into the scene. They cannot be healed and disappear at 0 HP, leaving no body. Ordinary unsummoned creatures retain their own healing rules.

Summoned forms remain tangible: they occupy squares, block movement, take damage and can be pushed or grappled normally unless their card says otherwise. Their energy composition grants no automatic incorporeality or damage/control immunity.

Summons require commands; see the @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.9ff12960a5e160cc]{summoning reference}. Without a command they do nothing, including following, lookout and alerts. Old orders grant no continued activity; existing conditions and durations still resolve. No free independent turns, inherent Reactions or summon chains. No count cap. Beyond 6 squares from the controller they disappear, including forced movement of either participant. Measure between the nearest occupied squares of controller and summon, using ordinary grid distance; this applies to every footprint. Exactly 6 squares is within the tether; beyond 6 causes immediate disappearance.

Summoned healing: the controller pays the healing ability’s printed SP cost instead of the summon, once, before resolution. The controller must have sufficient SP. Use the summon’s printed attribute and outcomes. Ordinary unsummoned healers pay their own cost.

Ordinary travel has no routine roll and no exhaustion track. Group checks occur outside combat only: each participant adds 1/2/3 to a declared target. State binary or cumulative before rolling. Make crafting and treatment rolls individually.

Safe overnight rest restores HP and SP; first aid uses one recipient allowance between rests. Scars are descriptive; Grit is gained once at levels 1/3/7 and never refreshes. At 0 HP heroes enter Dying; further damage causes an immediate Fortitude death roll. Weak adds a failure, Strong adds a success and Standard changes neither tally. Three failures kill unless Grit or an ability intervenes. Three successes stabilize at 0 HP. See @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.9303127ab1b28c3b]{recovery} for the complete procedure.

See @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.f5003d6e49eeed0c]{session resolution} for perception and timing, @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.b8dbac21301a8aa3]{conditions} and @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.401d23f4b66980ee]{scars} for their effects, and @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.7039600a66195489]{encounters} to plan a fight.

Player rolls — agreed

When a player looks for something, the DA calls for Reason, with Boons/Banes for circumstances. When someone might perceive a hidden player character, that player rolls Agility to remain Hidden. Do not add an opposed observer roll. Ordinary obvious information requires no roll. Hidden remains universal; actual concealment and a plausible approach matter.

Procedure: active searching or attempting to hide during combat costs a Main Action unless a card states otherwise. A hidden creature that attacks or openly reveals itself loses Hidden. No roll conceals someone in plain view with no plausible concealment. Establish progress and consequences before an unscripted roll. A Weak search might narrow the location; a Weak hiding attempt might reach cover while leaving evidence. These examples do not override the scene or a card’s printed outcomes.

Opportunities — agreed

Starting a provoking action triggers the opportunity attack before that action resolves. A hero uses Basic Melee with a held melee weapon or Basic Unarmed with a free hand. A DA creature uses its bestiary Basic Melee. Use the usual single-roll procedure for that attack. Then the original action continues if its actor is still capable; otherwise it stops. Damage alone does not automatically cancel the action. Forced movement never provokes.

Leaving melee reach voluntarily, including by crawling, can provoke. Casting a spell beside an enemy, standing, stowing and retrieving items can also provoke. Drawing as part of an attack stays part of that attack. Timing: commit the action when declared; check targets and capability again after interruption; pay an additional printed SP/HP/item cost only when continuing into its resolution. If interrupted permanently, the committed action is spent but an unspent potion or SP or HP cost is not consumed.

Player-controlled creatures — agreed

Creature cards must print attack and defense attributes. The controlling player rolls those printed creature attributes, not their character’s attribute. When an NPC attacks a player-controlled summon, its controller rolls the summon’s defense. When the summon attacks, its controller makes the attack roll. Use the ordinary single-roll attack/defense outcome mapping. A player-controlled attacker does not also cause a second player defense roll.

A summon disappears when its controller becomes unconscious or dies. An uncommanded summon does nothing; existing effects and conditions still resolve.

NPC-only resolution — approved October 16, 2026

Either a player or the DA assuming the player role can roll for NPC-only actions. For an NPC attacking another NPC, roll the defending NPC’s printed attribute named by the attack, with the applicable modifiers. Read the attacking creature’s Weak / Standard / Strong defense outcomes. Make only one roll, not an opposed pair.

For consequential NPC healing or another task, the same choice of roller uses the acting NPC’s printed attribute and outcomes. This does not transfer control of the NPC to the person handling the dice. Existing player-character and player-controlled creature procedures remain unchanged.

For example, when a bandit attacks an allied guard with an Agility-defense attack, a player or the DA rolls the guard’s Agility defense and reads the bandit’s card. Off-screen events may be resolved by DA judgment without rolling through unseen combat.

Stability and ordinary movement

Stability — approved: all characters and creatures start at 0; only an explicit trait, ability or item raises it, maximum 3, highest source only. It consumes forced movement once for the initial target and once for each new creature struck in a collision chain. Stop when movement is exhausted; never charge a creature twice. It does not resist Prone, grapples or conditions. See @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.3292b6a49dcf7236]{Stability} for a worked example. Collision timing approved October 16, 2026: resolve contact collision damage from movement remaining on arrival, then deduct the new member’s Stability before further travel. Applicable resistance still reduces damage.

Agreed: falling deals 3 HP per 2 squares fallen. Rounding and damage: use 3 × floor(distance / 2), physical damage with ordinary physical resistance; falls under 2 squares deal no automatic damage. Exceptional landing surfaces and circumstances are DA rulings.

Agreed: climbing and swimming use difficult-terrain movement cost, normally 2 per square, unless an ability changes it. Impossible surfaces and impassable currents do not become traversable merely by spending movement. Roll only when uncertainty has consequences. Cards can improve the ordinary activity.

Jumping — approved: broad jump up to max(1, 2 + Agility) squares; high jump up to max(0, 1 + floor(Agility / 2)) squares. Each square traveled spends movement; a broad jump needs 2 squares of approach, otherwise halve its maximum, rounded down (minimum 1). A high jump needs no approach. Land in a legal supported free square; no extra movement or passage through barriers. Negative Agility can mean no full square of high-jump clearance, not inability to hop over a small obstacle. Obstacles below a square and risky landings are adjudicated normally. No roll for a clear, safe jump within these limits; risky execution can call for Agility. These values are approved; specialist movement cards retain their explicit exceptions.

Consequence vocabulary

A consequence is what is at stake: harm, lost time, exposure, lost supplies, a worsened position or an opportunity that closes. A complication introduces an additional problem while retaining whatever progress the roll achieved. A benefit adds a useful advantage. State the stakes before rolling. Weak is progress, not automatic success; Strong is success with the printed result. Natural 111 adds a complication to Weak; 666 adds a benefit to Strong.

Use 1 Bane for a meaningful obstacle, 2 for a severe obstacle, 3 for an exceptional obstacle that remains possible. Use Boons symmetrically for real help or advantageous circumstances. These are DA guidance bands, not target numbers. Cancel Boons/Banes and apply the existing net cap of 3. Do not roll impossible attempts or apply the same obstacle twice under different names. Group progress and binary/cumulative task targets keep their existing rules.

Magic and healing

Use the @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.684bcf0a86d4b4b4]{spellbook rules} for casting, Rituals, sustain and cancellation. A character can unravel a casting through an ability that names a cancellation procedure. Its usual target is 2 + the affected spell's printed SP cost.

Healing aimed at a creature whose profile says healing harms it becomes a Life attack. Keep the spell's action, range, free hand and SP cost. Resolve its printed healing values as Life damage, using the hero's class casting attribute or the target's applicable player defense. Recovery benefits apply only to healing.

Approved by Bruce, October 13, 2026. Every character and creature starts with Stability 0. An ancestry trait, ability, equipment card or printed creature trait must explicitly grant a higher value. Stability is not calculated from attributes, ancestry size, armor, HP or level. Use the highest applicable grant, never their sum, to a maximum of 3.

Stability consumes the movement of a push, pull, slide or throw, minimum 0. Apply the initial target’s Stability once before it moves. When the moving group strikes a new creature, that creature’s Stability consumes remaining movement once as it joins the chain, after contact collision damage resolves. If none remains, the group stops. Never charge the same creature twice during one forced movement, even if several occupied squares collide.

Stability does not resist Prone, grappling, conditions or damage. It does not reduce voluntary movement or a thrown projectile’s range. A printed push of 1 can therefore move a Stability-0 target but not a Stability-1 target; its other effects still resolve. A stopped push does not erase the attack’s damage or conditions.

Example: a push of 5 strikes a creature with Stability 1, leaving 4. It moves one normal square, leaving 3, then strikes a creature with Stability 2. That new contact deals 3 collision damage to both participants, subject to applicable resistance. The newly struck creature’s Stability then consumes 2, leaving 1 for the moving group: enough to move one more normal square before stopping.

Use the existing terrain and collision rules. Spending Stability does not itself create damage. Collision timing — approved October 16, 2026: resolve contact collision damage using the movement remaining on arrival, then deduct the new member’s Stability before further travel. This preserves an impact even when the new member stops the chain. Stability resists displacement; applicable resistance reduces damage.

Crowded moving groups — approved October 16, 2026

Move the group together along the forced-movement path. Its members must finish in separate legal spaces. If the group cannot fit, stop at the last position where everyone can fit. The DA determines the exact arrangement.

Placement cannot send a creature through a wall or grant extra forward movement. Resolve any bounce after placing the group. Follow the @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.83082c8f9728466c]{collision rules} for impacts and a blocked bounce. Placement does not erase an impact.

The road matters. So do the people at its end. A warm welcome, a sound bridge and a name remembered at the right moment can carry your company farther than another weapon. Your abilities include ways to navigate these scenes, but you always begin with what your hero says and does.

Tell the DA what you examine, how you approach, and what you hope to learn. If lifting the rug reveals the trapdoor, you find it by lifting the rug. No perception roll is needed to discover a fact your action plainly reveals.

When searching involves uncertainty and a meaningful consequence, the DA calls for Reason. When someone might perceive your concealed hero, roll Agility to remain Hidden; the observer does not make an opposed roll. You need a plausible place to hide. Dice do not make you disappear in open view.

The road matters. So do the people at its end. A warm welcome, a sound bridge and a name remembered at the right moment can carry your company farther than another weapon. Your abilities include ways to navigate these scenes, but you always begin with what your hero says and does.

Explore with purpose

Tell the DA what you examine, how you approach, and what you hope to learn. If lifting the rug reveals the trapdoor, you find it by lifting the rug. No perception roll is needed to discover a fact your action plainly reveals.

When searching involves uncertainty and a meaningful consequence, the DA calls for Reason. When someone might perceive your concealed hero, roll Agility to remain Hidden; the observer does not make an opposed roll. You need a plausible place to hide. Dice do not make you disappear in open view.

Active searching or attempting to hide in combat costs a Main Action unless an ability says otherwise. Hidden is universal, not separately tracked for each observer. Attacking or openly revealing yourself ends it. The DA judges whether movement maintains actual concealment. Invisible is different: you cannot be seen, but your location is not necessarily unknown.

Before an unscripted roll, establish what progress means and what the consequences are. A Weak search might narrow the location without exposing the answer; a Weak concealment attempt might reach cover while leaving evidence of where you went. These examples are possibilities, not automatic effects that override the scene.

Consequences that matter

A consequence is what is at stake: injury, lost time, exposure, spent supplies, a worse position or a closing opportunity. A complication adds a problem while preserving any progress already earned. A benefit gives a useful advantage. The DA explains the stakes before asking for the roll.

If you can repeat an attempt indefinitely without cost, danger or changed circumstances, the table may be better served by describing the time and completing it. If failure would seal an escape route or alert a guard, say so before rolling. Weak always means its stated progress, not an unannounced success or an automatic failure.

Work as a group

Group checks occur outside combat. The DA sets a progress target and states whether the task is binary or cumulative. Each participating character rolls an appropriate attribute, contributing 1 progress on Weak, 2 on Standard, or 3 on Strong. Add the contributions and compare the total to the target.

For a binary task, meet the target in that attempt or the task is not completed. For a cumulative task, retain progress between attempts as the task allows. The DA states the time and consequence of each attempt. You can provide Aid or contribute your own group roll, not both to the same attempt.

> Example — the swollen gate. Three heroes heave against a gate before a patrol > arrives. The DA sets a binary target of 7. Weak, Strong and Strong contribute > 1 + 3 + 3 = 7: the gate opens. Weak, Standard and Strong would total 6; the gate > would stay shut and the declared consequence would follow. Pushing a boulder > uphill might instead retain those 6 progress for a later attempt.

Crafting, deriving recipes and treatment do not use group checks. Their individual procedures and daily limits remain in force.

Travel and the outdoors

Ordinary travel does not require routine rolls, and HOL has no exhaustion track. The DA calls for a roll when weather, pursuit, a dangerous route or another specific circumstance creates a consequence. Supplies and time still matter. Decide what your company carries, shares, buys or obtains with its abilities.

Foraging expertise comes from an appropriate environment card. It is not a universal permission to identify every edible mushroom. Other heroes can still inspect the land, collect something they already recognize, or help in a way the scene permits. Specialist cards provide their own outcomes and limitations.

Climbing and swimming normally cost 2 movement per square, like difficult terrain. This does not make a sheer unsupported wall climbable or an impassable current safe. A specialist ability can improve the activity. Roll only when the execution is uncertain and the consequence matters.

Jumping and falling

A running broad jump reaches max(1, 2 + Agility) squares. It needs two squares of approach; without that approach, halve the maximum, rounding down to a minimum of 1. A high jump reaches max(0, 1 + floor(Agility ÷ 2)) squares and needs no approach. Spend movement for the distance traveled and land in a legal, supported, free square.

AgilityRunning broad jumpStanding broad jumpHigh jump

Zero high-jump squares does not mean you cannot hop over a low obstacle. The grid measures large clearances. Safe jumps within your limits need no roll; a risky landing can call for Agility. Jumping does not grant extra movement or passage through a barrier.

Falling deals 3 physical damage per complete 2 squares fallen. Round the distance down to complete pairs before multiplying; normal physical resistance applies. A fall of 5 squares deals 6 damage before resistance. A fall under 2 squares has no automatic falling damage. Exceptional surfaces and landing circumstances are DA rulings.

Magic in your hands

Learn spells from the pages of your spellbooks. To cast one, spend its printed SP cost and follow its action and outcome. An attack spell deals its Weak damage on a Weak roll.

You choose a card before rolling. A line, rectangle or placed area must use its printed dimensions and range. Connected placed squares share edges. Decide targets and any damage-type choice before rolling. An illustration or evocative description does not silently make the area larger or add a condition.

To unravel a spell, use a spell or ability that supplies cancellation progress. The usual target is 2 + the affected spell's printed SP cost. Casting beside an enemy can provoke an opportunity attack. Resolve it before paying SP and continuing the spell.

Beast forms keep your own HP, attributes and scars. They are not replaceable HP pools. Use the form's printed actions and equipment restrictions. A form does not import an entire monster entry or grant spellcasting if its rules forbid it.

For casting actions, Rituals, sustained magic and spellbook learning, use @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.684bcf0a86d4b4b4]{Magic and spellbooks}.

Healing spends spell points

Each spell costs its printed SP. The first spell in each spellbook costs 0 SP. Calculate your reserve using @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.d7def8e34dfcb560]{Starting SP} in Chapter 2. Pay the full SP cost before rolling, after resolving any opportunity attack. Healing requires a free hand. Restore the printed HP, apply the recipient's Life resistance, and restore at least 1 if HP is missing. Never exceed maximum HP. A Dying or stabilized living recipient needs no consent or Reaction. Ordinary healing erases no scars and cannot restore the dead; only an explicit resurrection working can do so. Potions use their own fixed healing and inventory die, without a spell outcome roll or SP cost.

> Example: a finite reserve. A Shepherd with 6 SP spends 1 SP to cast Cure Wounds. A Standard result heals 5 HP, reduced to 3 by the recipient's Life resistance 2. The healer has 5 SP left. Restoring HP cannot replenish SP.

A healing spell can attack a creature whose profile says healing harms it. Use the hero’s casting attribute and the spell’s range and SP cost. Its HP result becomes Life damage; beneficial recovery riders do not help that target. Use the ordinary player-roll procedure, without a second opposed save.

Make and identify items

A recipe tells you what you can make, what it takes and how you learn it. Trail Workshop I teaches two recipes from its list. Trail Workshop II teaches two more. Teachers and discoveries can provide other recipes.

Gather the ingredients and complete the recipe's work interval on your own. Roll Knowledge when called for and apply progress or inventory steps as the recipe describes. A supply starts at d4 and grows up to the recipe's cap. Check the inventory die for any carried materials you used.

Inspect an unfamiliar item to learn what its appearance and ordinary use reveal. If the item requires deeper understanding, follow its instructions. The Identify spell in the @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.75ed761297e85e1b]{Detection spellbook} reveals a magical item's properties as described on its page.

Rest and development

The DA determines whether a place is safe enough to spend saved DP. Level awards are milestones, not payment for each defeated creature. Record your learned abilities, recipes, remaining DP and scars.

First Aid uses supplies and time. A Brief Rest restores 6 HP and 3 SP once per day. A Night’s Rest restores full HP and SP. An inn, a friendly workshop, a healer's garden or a camp among allies can become part of the story. Gather supplies before you leave, and note what the company still needs to replace.

A familiar greeting can open a door that gold cannot. An inscription can preserve an enemy's warning long after the enemy is dust. Languages tell you whom your hero can understand and which voices shaped their life. They do not determine ancestry, allegiance or character.

Choose your languages

Begin with Common and one other ordinary language learned in the community that raised you. Common is the campaign's shared trade language; the DA may give it a local name. Choose your other language with the DA from the list below or the campaign's equivalent. Any ancestry may know any language. Culture suggests where you learned it, rather than imposing a compulsory choice.

Record the language's actual name, not just “regional” or “community language.” If Common was your only home language, choose another ordinary language learned through neighbors, work or travel. Choose these starting languages for free alongside your culture and background.

Apply explicit extra grants afterward. A Foot in Two Worlds lets a Human choose another ancestry, learn one language native to it and gain one trait from its trait list, while keeping Human base HP and Speed. A signed language is an ordinary language when the campaign uses it. Follow any explicit restriction on a grant.

Unless a grant says otherwise, knowing a language includes speaking, understanding, and reading and writing its usual script, if it has one. A grant that specifically says spoken, understands or cannot speak keeps that restriction. Record such limits beside the language. Speaking a language does not require a separate skill rating, and attributes grant no automatic extra languages.

Ordinary languages

These are starting options, not a required history of the world. Their names describe familiar traditions; anyone raised among their speakers may learn them. Each row is one language unless it explicitly asks you to name a particular one.

LanguageWhere you might learn or encounter it
CommonMarkets, mixed settlements, roads and adventuring companies.
Regional languageChoose one named local language: a river kingdom, island community or frontier valley. Each is a separate choice.
DwarvenDeep halls, quarry towns and craft communities; records of lineage, work and agreements.
ElvenWoodland settlements and long-lived artistic traditions; songs, histories and correspondence.
HalflingHearth communities, traveling families and river villages; stories and everyday business.
GoblinGoblin communities and their neighbors; salvage yards, markets and warrens.
OrcOrc communities and their neighbors; border settlements, expeditions and oral histories.
GiantGiant communities and peoples who trade with them; landmarks, stone records and remembered journeys.
KoboldKobold communities and their neighbors; tunnel works, workshops and trading posts.
Harbor CantMultilingual ports and ship crews. A full local language, not universal knowledge of every sailor's slang.
Way SignA complete signed language shared by participating communities. Communication requires sight and usable signing gestures.

Uncommon and ancient languages

These languages are not included in an unrestricted ordinary language grant. Choose one only when a grant explicitly allows it or the DA makes it an ordinary option for the campaign before character creation. Their availability reflects the setting, not a higher numerical bonus.

LanguageWhere it becomes useful
DraconicSpeaking with dragons and their learned allies; reading draconic inscriptions. Kobold is a separate language.
FeyNegotiating with fey courts and woodland powers; understanding their stories and spoken bargains.
InfernalSpeaking with fiends and interpreting their correspondence or contracts. Knowing it does not bind or summon anything.
CelestialConversations with celestial beings and some sacred traditions. It grants no divine authority.
ElementalSpeech used by elemental beings capable of language. It does not let you command fire, weather or an unintelligent elemental.
Elder TongueChoose one named lost or ancient scholarly language. Different vanished civilizations need not share it.

A sacred text may be written in Common, Dwarven or any other language. “Sacred,” “scholarly” and “courtly” describe use, not automatic additional languages. Beasts' calls, a spirit's images and a construct's signal lights are forms of communication, not languages you gain by choosing a row in these tables.

Use languages at the table

When you share a language and can hear, see or read it as required, ordinary communication needs no roll. State what you say or ask. A conversation can still involve uncertainty about persuasion, deception or evidence; use the normal attribute or the ability you declared. Knowing the words does not make the listener agree, reveal secrets or recognize your authority.

A language barrier is not simply extra Banes on a roll. Without a shared means of communication, you cannot deliver a precise argument merely by rolling well. Pointing, drawing or demonstrating can convey something simple: “danger there,” “follow me,” or an offered trade. Agree on what is actually understood. An interpreter, a translation, or an applicable ability can make a more complicated exchange possible. A card that explicitly requires a shared language still requires one; an interpreter does not silently change its target requirement.

Reading a clear message in a language you can read needs no roll. Damaged text, an unfamiliar technical subject or a cipher may present a separate problem. Sharing an alphabet does not grant another language, and a cipher is not an extra language choice. Ask the DA what evidence or expertise could make progress possible.

Translate the Fragment supplies a way to interpret unfamiliar written text. Use its printed time, progress and outcomes. Completing a translation does not teach you the whole language. A copied voice or disguise likewise supplies no vocabulary or memories unless its ability explicitly says so.

Keep learning grounded

Record new languages when an explicit trait, ability or agreed campaign grant provides them. To pursue fluency through a teacher, a community or useful texts, agree with the DA on the time and any cost before you begin. Record the language when you complete that agreement. In the meantime, a translation or an interpreter can help you understand a particular message or conversation.

> At the gate. An elf raised in a dwarven mining town chooses Common and > Dwarven. She reads the quarry's warning without a roll. Its damaged diagram > still needs investigation. Her human companion chose Goblin for A Foot in Two > Worlds and learned Goblin; he can question a salvager and read the written ledger.

Repairing a gate, following a trail or winning a reluctant listener’s trust may take several attempts. Agree with the DA on what you want to accomplish and how you will approach it. Track your progress toward that objective. You can contribute through ordinary actions or use a learned ability for its listed benefits.

Set the objective before rolling

The Dungeon Architect states the concrete result, what evidence or resources are needed, and how much progress completes it. Use 3 progress for a modest task, 6 for a substantial task, 9 for a demanding task and 12 for an exceptional task. The DA chooses a target that fits the task and explains what makes your approach possible. If you need a tool, evidence or a different approach before you can proceed, establish that first.

The DA also states the work interval, deadline and known consequences. A printed ability supplies its own interval and progress results. An ordinary feasible contribution adds 1/2/3 progress with the attribute appropriate to the approach. Progress is shared only when contributions genuinely serve the same objective. Another person may Aid or make their own contribution during an interval, not both. Craft projects remain individual.

When you reach the target, accomplish the agreed result. Count progress toward that objective only. A Weak roll adds its stated progress. Natural retained 111 also adds a complication, and 666 adds a benefit. Apply any consequences established before the attempt, including a deadline or approaching danger.

Social encounters

State the concession sought and who can grant it. The DA determines whether persuasion, evidence, deception, a bargain or pressure can work. Set one objective for listeners who share a motive; use separate objectives for listeners with different interests. State known boundaries and deal-breakers before the roll when the characters could recognize them.

An exchange is one meaningful statement or response, normally about a minute outside combat. In combat, an exchange costs a Main Action. Listeners must be able to perceive and understand the approach. A new roll needs a new relevant fact, offer, demonstration or changed circumstance. Repeating the same argument earns no progress. Different speakers cannot obtain extra rolls by repeating it.

Completing the objective earns the agreed concession. The listener keeps their own motives, and each player decides what their hero thinks and does. Agree on an attainable concession before rolling. If circumstances change enough to require a new objective, the DA explains what changed and why the existing progress no longer answers the problem. A permitted Weak roll still advances the objective.

Example: a keeper needs assurance before opening a gate. The DA sets 6 progress to gain entry, requiring a credible reason and a guarantee against trouble. A Standard learned appeal contributes 3. A companion presents a relevant letter and rolls Standard on an ordinary Reason contribution for 2. The first speaker adds a new offer and rolls Weak for 1: the gate opens under the agreed terms.

Your HP measures how much danger you can endure before you fall. Rest, treatment and magic restore it. Grit is the courage that brings you back when ordinary endurance fails. Scars remember what happened after the numbers recover.

At level 1, maximum HP is 10 + ancestry HP contribution + class HP contribution + Fortitude + explicit HP benefits. At every later level, add the ancestry and class contributions again. Each contribution is 1, 2 or 3; record their sum as your HP gain per level. Fortitude and fixed benefits apply once.

For level 1 or higher: maximum HP = 10 + level × (ancestry + class HP contributions) + Fortitude + explicit HP benefits. On gaining a level, increase current HP by the same amount as maximum HP; this does not end Dying or restore HP to a character at 0. Such a character gains the maximum only until recovered.

Your HP measures how much danger you can endure before you fall. Rest, treatment and magic restore it. Grit is the courage that brings you back when ordinary endurance fails. Scars remember what happened after the numbers recover.

HP and growing endurance

At level 1, maximum HP is 10 + ancestry HP contribution + class HP contribution + Fortitude + explicit HP benefits. At every later level, add the ancestry and class contributions again. Each contribution is 1, 2 or 3; record their sum as your HP gain per level. Fortitude and fixed benefits apply once.

For level 1 or higher: maximum HP = 10 + level × (ancestry + class HP contributions) + Fortitude + explicit HP benefits. On gaining a level, increase current HP by the same amount as maximum HP; this does not end Dying or restore HP to a character at 0. Such a character gains the maximum only until recovered.

Damage reduces current HP, to a minimum of 0. Healing restores the stated amount, up to maximum HP. Apply Life resistance to magical healing and potions, with a minimum of 1 actual healing when HP is missing. First aid and rest are not Life magic and ignore Life resistance. Healing cannot restore the dead.

Falling to 0 HP

A player character reduced from positive HP to 0 enters Dying, falls prone and becomes unconscious. Start each Dying episode with zero failure marks and zero success marks. Ordinary NPCs and creatures normally die at 0. Summoned forms disappear.

At the start of each Dying turn, make a Fortitude death roll using 3d6 and the usual Boons and Banes. Use only the result band for this roll, even on retained triples.

Death-roll resultEffect
WeakAdd 1 failure mark.
StandardKeep both tallies as they are.
StrongAdd 1 success mark.

Track failures and successes separately throughout the episode. On your third success, stabilize at 0 HP and clear both tallies. On your third failure, you die unless you spend Grit or an ability intervenes at its stated trigger.

Last Words. If your hero dies, you can describe their final words, gesture or silence as part of that moment.

Further damage

Taking damage while already at 0 HP causes one immediate death roll per event. An event that deals 0 damage leaves the tallies alone. Apply the death roll's result once for the whole event. Later events such as Bleeding or Burning each trigger their own roll. Damage while stabilized first returns you to Dying, then causes this immediate roll. The event that first reduces positive HP to 0 does not also cause an immediate death roll.

Resolve the damage and immediate death roll before moving on to the next event. If healing or Grit restores positive HP, later damage reduces that HP normally. Keep turn timing until Dying and immediate hazards have been resolved; ending a battle does not skip death rolls.

Stabilization and recovery at 0

Anyone can use the Stabilize Maneuver on an adjacent Dying hero, without a roll or supplies. Clear both tallies and end Dying, leaving them at 0 HP. They regain consciousness from HP loss, but remain prone and cannot take Main Actions, Maneuvers, Reactions or voluntary movement until they regain HP. Apply the same three defense Banes as Unconscious while at 0. They can speak, perceive their surroundings and accept help. Companions can carry them. Another source of unconsciousness or incapacity still follows its own remedy.

A stabilized hero makes no turn-start death rolls. Further damage restarts Dying. Healing above 0 ends Dying, clears both tallies and ends HP-caused unconsciousness; it does not automatically stand the hero up or remove other conditions. Healing may target a Dying or stabilized hero without requiring consent or a Reaction.

Grit: three chances across a career

Gain 1 Grit at level 1, 1 more at level 3, and 1 more at level 7. Record each grant and each expenditure. Grit never refreshes through rest, treatment, magic or a new session. Unspent points carry forward; spending one removes it permanently. These milestones are the only Grit grants.

Spend one Grit when you fall to 0, at the start of a Dying turn, immediately after a death roll adds a failure mark (including the third failure), or while stabilized at 0. This costs no action or Reaction. Set current HP to half maximum HP, rounded up, clear both tallies, and end Dying and HP-caused unconsciousness. Other conditions remain. If an ability makes HP unavailable for recovery, apply that limit to Grit as well.

> Example — a third failure. You have 17 maximum HP, two failures and one > success. You roll Weak. Before death becomes final, you spend your last Grit. > Set HP to 9 and clear both tallies.

Scars tell the story

Surviving an incident in which you reached 0 HP leaves a permanent descriptive scar. Choose it with the DA once the danger has passed: a pale seam, singed hair, a shaking hand when thunder sounds, or a remembered voice. One incident can include several falls and rescues; it leaves one scar, rather than a new entry for every hit at 0. A later incident can add another.

A scar changes no attribute, HP, movement, Boons, Banes or future death rolls. It cannot require a treatment track or remove a body part. Its emotional meaning belongs to the player. Treatment and healing restore capability without erasing history. See @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.401d23f4b66980ee]{Scars and Survival} for prompts.

Brief Rest

After one uninterrupted hour in a place the DA judges safe, restore 6 HP and 3 SP, up to your maximums. You can gain this recovery once per day. A Dying hero must be stabilized before recovering from rest.

You can add First Aid and learned Spellcraft Recovery to this recovery. Use the supplies, time and allowance each activity calls for. Another hero can tend your wounds while you rest. If your activities need more time than the rest provides, take the extra time to finish them.

Night’s Rest

A Night’s Rest is the safe overnight rest referred to by abilities and spells.

After eight hours in a place the DA judges safe, with food, water and adequate shelter, restore full HP and SP and renew your first-aid allowance and learned recovery uses that refresh overnight. Include at least six hours of sleep or equivalent rest; the other two can include quiet activity or a watch. Oath-Bound use the same rest period, with stillness in place of sleep. You can gain these benefits only once in 24 hours.

A fight, strenuous work or forced travel interrupts the rest; complete a new uninterrupted period afterward. Brief waking, conversation and routine watch do not. The DA explains what makes a campsite unsafe before the group commits to it. A stabilized hero can recover this way; a Dying hero must first be stabilized.

Grit stays spent, scars remain and lasting conditions follow their own remedies.

First aid and treatment

Stabilization is the immediate rescue. First Aid is slower care that anyone can provide: spend ten uninterrupted minutes, use one supply of clean dressings and medicine, and make a Knowledge roll for yourself or one willing, Dying or stabilized living creature within reach. Restore 2/4/6 HP on Weak/Standard/Strong. Resolve the supply's inventory die after use. A Dying patient continues making death rolls during treatment. Stabilize them first when possible.

Each recipient can receive one treatment attempt between safe overnight rests, shared by all healers. Use ordinary first aid or a learned treatment such as Field Dressing for that attempt. Mark the allowance and use the supply when you begin, then restore HP when you finish. You can stabilize someone or reduce a condition separately. Treat starred conditions with the remedy listed by their source.

Magical healing and spell points

Your SP reserve is separate from HP. Your level contributes 2 × level SP: 2 at level 1, 6 at level 3 and 14 at level 7. Add your ancestry’s SP contribution and twice your positive class casting attribute. An attribute of 0 or less contributes 0 SP. Add any increases learned through Spellcraft’s Soul Capacity or Mind Capacity paths and other explicit SP benefits. From level 2 onward, gain 2 maximum SP each level. These increases enlarge capacity without restoring spent SP. Track current SP separately. A safe overnight rest fills the reserve; learned recovery follows its own timing.

Healing magic spends the caster's printed SP cost before resolution, whether used in battle or during quiet time. Keep a free hand and follow the spell's range. Cast as often as you have the SP and time. The recipient keeps their first-aid allowance for treatment. For a potion, use its printed healing and check its inventory die.

A summoned healer's controller pays the SP cost. Summoned energy forms cannot receive healing and disappear at 0 HP. No ability may turn HP healing into SP recovery unless it explicitly supplies that conversion.

Conditions keep their own rules

At turn end, resolve a temporary numbered condition, then reduce its rating by 1. A starred contribution has no automatic decay; use its source's remedy. Keep starred and temporary contributions separate. Scars never apply conditions.

Spend a Main Action and use a plausible method to reduce Bleeding, Burning or Freezing on yourself or an adjacent creature by 1, without a roll. This does not heal HP or consume first aid. Other conditions use their own removal procedures. A curse can persist through an overnight rest even though the hero's HP returns.

A non-player healer without a separately printed SP reserve has 6 SP. Summoned forms use their controller’s reserve instead.

Record each condition affecting your hero and its rating, if it has one. Use the reference below to see what it changes and how it ends.

Ratings, decay, and persistence

At the end of the affected character's turn, resolve a temporary numbered condition's effect, then reduce its rating by 1. At 0 it ends. A condition gained during that turn also decreases at that turn's end. Numbered instances add where meaningful; binary states do not. Normal Boon/Bane cancellation and caps apply.

The number can describe severity as well as duration (Dazed, Burning), or duration only (Blinded, Paralyzed). A higher duration-only rating does not strengthen the condition. Dazed 3 or greater grants no action categories.

An asterisk means no automatic decay: Blinded 1* is blindness that persists until its specified remedy. It does not mean every such injury is incurable. The source states which remedy removes it. Maintained Grappled does not decay. Binary conditions and lasting effects use their own removal rules.

Spend a Main Action to reduce an appropriate condition on yourself or an adjacent creature by 1 without a roll: staunch Bleeding, extinguish Burning, or warm someone suffering Freezing with a plausible method. This is not a universal cure for every condition. Specialist abilities can remove more or use a cheaper action. A star prevents automatic decay, not a removal method explicitly allowed by its source. Record temporary and starred contributions separately, using the mixed-source tracking procedure below.

Example: untreated Bleeding 3 deals 3 damage, decreases to 2, then deals 2 and 1 on subsequent turns before ending. A Main Action reducing it before the first tick changes that sequence to 2, then 1. Matching resistance can reduce a Burning or Freezing tick to 0. Matching damage immunity also makes it 0. The condition still decays normally. Immunity to the condition prevents it from applying.

Temporary and lasting conditions

A temporary numbered contribution resolves and decays at the end of the affected creature's turn. A starred contribution has no automatic decay. A lasting effect remains until its printed remedy. Maintained Grappled and binary Prone instead use their own release, escape or standing rules.

An asterisk means persistent, not necessarily incurable. Follow the ability or hazard's remedy. Temporary Blinded 2 clears after two end-of-turn decay steps; Blinded 1* from a curse remains until that curse's remedy is met. Safe overnight rest restores HP but does not override that remedy. Scars apply no conditions.

Asleep, Paralyzed, Unconscious, and Petrified apply three defense Banes; overlapping helpless states apply that penalty once. Dazed adds no defense Banes. Attacks against a Grappled creature gain one Boon per level of its Grappled rating, including attacks against grapplers, using normal Boon/Bane rules. When Dazed and Grappled coexist, use the greater action restriction, not their sum.

Grappling restricts the grappler by their own contribution as well as the target. Multiple grapplers' contributions add on the target. Each can freely release even at rating 3, ending their contribution. An outside intervention can break a hold by separating the grappler from the target beyond its reach or rendering the grappler unconscious. A creature at Grappled 3 or higher can be cuffed by an adjacent character using a Maneuver and suitable @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.da003d91ba817502]{restraints}. Once the captive is secured and combat is over, resolve the scene through ordinary narration.

Example: Paralyzed 3 prevents actions and movement, falls to 2 at turn end, then to 1, then clears. Dazed 3 instead gradually returns action options as it decays. Blinded 2 is full blindness for two decay steps, not stronger blindness than 1.

While Prone, use the crawling and standing costs above. Prone alone changes no attack or defense dice.
