When conditions affect actions

Dazed and Grappled determine retained action categories at the start of the affected creature’s turn. Changes during the turn do not undo spent actions or recalculate that turn’s category selection. Temporary Dazed decays at turn end; maintained Grappled does not decay. Grappled’s movement restriction still applies while the hold exists. Paralyzed, Asleep and Unconscious retain their immediate restrictions; they are not action-category selection effects.

Mixed-source tracking: record temporary and starred contributions separately. Add effective severity where the condition uses severity; decay only the temporary part. For duration-only conditions, either positive contribution keeps the condition active, without multiplying its effect. Generic temporary reduction removes temporary rating only; permanent treatment follows its source.

Your HP measures how much danger you can endure before you fall. Rest, treatment and magic restore it. Grit is the courage that brings you back when ordinary endurance fails. Scars remember what happened after the numbers recover.

HP and growing endurance

At level 1, maximum HP is 10 + ancestry HP contribution + class HP contribution + Fortitude + explicit HP benefits. At every later level, add the ancestry and class contributions again. Each contribution is 1, 2 or 3; record their sum as your HP gain per level. Fortitude and fixed benefits apply once.

For level 1 or higher: maximum HP = 10 + level × (ancestry + class HP contributions) + Fortitude + explicit HP benefits. On gaining a level, increase current HP by the same amount as maximum HP; this does not end Dying or restore HP to a character at 0. Such a character gains the maximum only until recovered.

Damage reduces current HP, to a minimum of 0. Healing restores the stated amount, up to maximum HP. Apply Life resistance to magical healing and potions, with a minimum of 1 actual healing when HP is missing. First aid and rest are not Life magic and ignore Life resistance. Healing cannot restore the dead.

Falling to 0 HP

A player character reduced from positive HP to 0 enters Dying, falls prone and becomes unconscious. Start each Dying episode with zero failure marks and zero success marks. Ordinary NPCs and creatures normally die at 0. Summoned forms disappear.

At the start of each Dying turn, make a Fortitude death roll using 3d6 and the usual Boons and Banes. Use only the result band for this roll, even on retained triples.

Death-roll resultEffect
WeakAdd 1 failure mark.
StandardKeep both tallies as they are.
StrongAdd 1 success mark.

Track failures and successes separately throughout the episode. On your third success, stabilize at 0 HP and clear both tallies. On your third failure, you die unless you spend Grit or an ability intervenes at its stated trigger.

Last Words. If your hero dies, you can describe their final words, gesture or silence as part of that moment.

Further damage

Taking damage while already at 0 HP causes one immediate death roll per event. An event that deals 0 damage leaves the tallies alone. Apply the death roll's result once for the whole event. Later events such as Bleeding or Burning each trigger their own roll. Damage while stabilized first returns you to Dying, then causes this immediate roll. The event that first reduces positive HP to 0 does not also cause an immediate death roll.

Resolve the damage and immediate death roll before moving on to the next event. If healing or Grit restores positive HP, later damage reduces that HP normally. Keep turn timing until Dying and immediate hazards have been resolved; ending a battle does not skip death rolls.

Stabilization and recovery at 0

Anyone can use the Stabilize Maneuver on an adjacent Dying hero, without a roll or supplies. Clear both tallies and end Dying, leaving them at 0 HP. They regain consciousness from HP loss, but remain prone and cannot take Main Actions, Maneuvers, Reactions or voluntary movement until they regain HP. Apply the same three defense Banes as Unconscious while at 0. They can speak, perceive their surroundings and accept help. Companions can carry them. Another source of unconsciousness or incapacity still follows its own remedy.

A stabilized hero makes no turn-start death rolls. Further damage restarts Dying. Healing above 0 ends Dying, clears both tallies and ends HP-caused unconsciousness; it does not automatically stand the hero up or remove other conditions. Healing may target a Dying or stabilized hero without requiring consent or a Reaction.

Grit: three chances across a career

Gain 1 Grit at level 1, 1 more at level 3, and 1 more at level 7. Record each grant and each expenditure. Grit never refreshes through rest, treatment, magic or a new session. Unspent points carry forward; spending one removes it permanently. These milestones are the only Grit grants.

Spend one Grit when you fall to 0, at the start of a Dying turn, immediately after a death roll adds a failure mark (including the third failure), or while stabilized at 0. This costs no action or Reaction. Set current HP to half maximum HP, rounded up, clear both tallies, and end Dying and HP-caused unconsciousness. Other conditions remain. If an ability makes HP unavailable for recovery, apply that limit to Grit as well.

> Example — a third failure. You have 17 maximum HP, two failures and one > success. You roll Weak. Before death becomes final, you spend your last Grit. > Set HP to 9 and clear both tallies.

Scars tell the story

Surviving an incident in which you reached 0 HP leaves a permanent descriptive scar. Choose it with the DA once the danger has passed: a pale seam, singed hair, a shaking hand when thunder sounds, or a remembered voice. One incident can include several falls and rescues; it leaves one scar, rather than a new entry for every hit at 0. A later incident can add another.

A scar changes no attribute, HP, movement, Boons, Banes or future death rolls. It cannot require a treatment track or remove a body part. Its emotional meaning belongs to the player. Treatment and healing restore capability without erasing history. See @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.401d23f4b66980ee]{Scars and Survival} for prompts.

Brief Rest

After one uninterrupted hour in a place the DA judges safe, restore 6 HP and 3 SP, up to your maximums. You can gain this recovery once per day. A Dying hero must be stabilized before recovering from rest.

You can add First Aid and learned Spellcraft Recovery to this recovery. Use the supplies, time and allowance each activity calls for. Another hero can tend your wounds while you rest. If your activities need more time than the rest provides, take the extra time to finish them.

Night’s Rest

A Night’s Rest is the safe overnight rest referred to by abilities and spells.

After eight hours in a place the DA judges safe, with food, water and adequate shelter, restore full HP and SP and renew your first-aid allowance and learned recovery uses that refresh overnight. Include at least six hours of sleep or equivalent rest; the other two can include quiet activity or a watch. Oath-Bound use the same rest period, with stillness in place of sleep. You can gain these benefits only once in 24 hours.

A fight, strenuous work or forced travel interrupts the rest; complete a new uninterrupted period afterward. Brief waking, conversation and routine watch do not. The DA explains what makes a campsite unsafe before the group commits to it. A stabilized hero can recover this way; a Dying hero must first be stabilized.

Grit stays spent, scars remain and lasting conditions follow their own remedies.

Coins and trade

HOL uses one currency: coins. A listed price buys the described ordinary item or full supply. When you learn an ability that requires ordinary gear, receive a compatible item free of charge. Share it between abilities that use the same equipment. Each hero begins with paid food, water, lighting, and one lesser healing potion. Return unwanted provisions for their full price during creation.

Useful intact gear sells for half its listed value, rounded down, or trades at full value with a willing trader. A 12-coin weapon sells for 6 or trades for 12 coins of goods. Pay any shortfall in coins; excess trade value is not cash change. A merchant does not have unlimited stock or an obligation to buy everything you make.

Armor and training

Light, medium, and heavy armor grant physical resistance 1, 2, and 3 while worn. If you lack the matching learned training, subtract the armor’s resistance rating from effective Agility. Use the highest applicable armor resistance and the largest Agility penalty from untrained worn armor. Recalculate Speed from effective Agility.

TrainingRequirementDPPhysical resistance
@UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.8906224eb8a6c4b3]{Light Armor I}Study Armor1Light: 1
Light Armor IIILight Armor I and II2Medium: 2
Heavy Armor ILight Armor III; level 33Heavy: 3

The Harness path develops armor training in order. Light Armor II costs 2 DP and improves your footing before Light Armor III teaches medium armor. Heavy armor begins at level 3. Each later training includes the armor categories you already know. Use the highest applicable resistance. Attacks deal at least 1 damage after resistance if any damaging component survives immunity.

Weapon training

Learn a technique that uses melee weapons, ranged weapons, thrown weapons, or unarmed attacks to train in that family. An entry that only mentions a weapon in passing grants no training. If you make a basic attack with a family you have not trained in, deal 1/1/2 physical damage on Weak, Standard, or Strong. Use the basic action’s printed damage when you have trained in its family. Apply resistance and damage immunity as usual.

Choose compatible ammunition for each ranged weapon. Check that supply after firing.

Bulk and hands

Record each carried item's Bulk. Most individual equipment entries and supply bundles use 1 Bulk; the entry tells you otherwise. A pack adds its own Bulk and does not erase its contents. Capacity is 10 + 3 × Brawn. Each Bulk above capacity reduces Speed by 1, to a minimum of 0.

A single compatible weapon serves all the attacks that can use it. Ordinary weapon appearance changes no mechanics. A flaming melee weapon can add its printed fire effect to a compatible attack; it cannot become a ranged weapon simply because you chose a ranged card.

Track occupied hands. Healing requires a free hand. A bow, two-handed weapon, or weapon-and-shield combination leaves none. Drawing for an attack is part of that attack, dropping is free, and proper stowing or picking up costs a Maneuver. There is no automatic free grip-change exception.

Inventory dice

A supply bundle has an inventory die instead of a counted number of uses. After using it, roll that die. On a 1, reduce it one step. On any other result it stays where it is. The use you just completed still works.

d20 → d12 → d10 → d8 → d6 → d4 → out

Check at the interval printed on the supply. Check ammunition after use, water each time you drink, food for each person-day consumed, and lighting each hour. A d4 healing bottle has a one-in-four chance of becoming empty after each use. It is not a promise of four doses.

> Example — the last swallow. You drink a lesser healing bottle and restore its > 6 HP, reduced by Life resistance if applicable. Then roll its d4 inventory die. > A 1 empties the bottle; you still received that healing. At full HP the bottle > cannot heal beyond your maximum.

Recipes and abilities such as Wild Harvest raise a supply by the listed number of steps. Start at d4 when replenishing an empty supply and stop at the printed cap. Refills from a suitable source bring the supply up to its starting die. Unmeasured leftovers stay part of the same supply when transferred to another container.

Special equipment and understanding

A special item adds only the effects it prints: damage, resistance, an ability or another explicit benefit. Apply normal nonstacking rules to matching numerical bonuses. Different damage-type resistances can coexist; use the highest of each.

The item states whether understanding is required. Identification abilities reveal different kinds of information. To make an item yourself, learn its recipe and gather the listed tools and materials. The recipe explains the work time and what each result produces.

Items that change attributes

Add a modifier. For each attribute, add the highest applicable item bonus and subtract the largest applicable item penalty. Published item modifiers range from −2 to +2. Your effective attribute can go beyond the creation range.

Cursed penalties. If a cursed item penalizes an attribute, apply the largest applicable item penalty and ignore item bonuses to that attribute while the curse applies.

Set a value. If an item sets an attribute to a specific value, use that exact value while the item applies. It replaces your base value and every bonus and penalty to that attribute. You can use one item that sets a given attribute at a time. Apply any exception printed on a curse card, such as suppressing item bonuses or taking precedence over other effects.

> With Brawn +1 and item bonuses of +2 and +1, your effective Brawn is +3. A cursed > item with a −1 Brawn penalty suppresses both bonuses and brings your Brawn to 0. > An item that sets Brawn to +3 gives you exactly +3 unless the curse overrides it.

All prices are whole coins, with no metal denominations. Prices establish a usable town market, not a historical currency conversion. Use the prices and supply rules below.

What a coin buys

A simple meal costs 1 coin. A plain bed costs 2 coins per night, meals separate. Ordinary local labor pays about 3 coins per day; skilled work about 6. These are guides for an ordinary town. Dangerous adventuring can earn more because the company takes greater risks.

Record any gear your character choices provide, then buy what you still need. Choose armor you have trained to wear. Use the damage of your chosen attack regardless of the weapon’s appearance. Prices for functionally equivalent ordinary melee weapons are equal; a jeweled hilt may be valuable decoration but does not hit harder.

Supplies and restocking

The printed price buys one full supply at its listed die, including an ordinary holder. Each healing bottle has a d4 supply. Choose Lesser, Greater or Superior for the amount of HP restored per use. After using a supply, roll its inventory die. On 1 it steps down. The use that empties it still works.

A d4 averages 4 uses before empty; d6 averages 10 total uses through its d4 stage; d8 averages 18. These are expectations, not guaranteed charges. The inventory die cannot be converted into an exact number of arrows or spoonfuls.

Shop refills: a shop can refill a supply to its printed starting die for its full listed supply price. Or buy a separate full supply at that price, which costs another Bulk. No discounted partial refill, die combining, decanting into fresh full-die bottles or cash credit for unknown leftovers. Crafting can increase a supply by the steps stated in its recipe. Refill a flask to d8 from a safe water source for free. A town may charge 1 coin for a refill.

Availability, selling and crafting

These prices assume a supplied town. Ordinary travel goods are common. Specialist tools, potions and unusual supplies need an appropriate seller. Special equipment prices are valuation benchmarks: the DA decides whether an item is actually on sale. No automatic stock refresh after a rest or new scene.

For an unusual shortage or remote seller, the DA may quote double ordinary prices; otherwise use the printed value rather than maintaining regional multipliers. Record a concrete offer before buying. Exact scarcity and merchant stock remain adventure decisions, not a universal cap on player purchases.

Selling and trading: intact, useful gear sells for half list price, rounded down, or trades for its full listed value with a willing trader. A 12-coin weapon sells for 6 coins or trades for 12 coins of goods. Pay any shortfall in coins; unused trade value is not cash change. A trade cannot be redeemed for coins, vouchers or other cash equivalents at full value. Card-granted items use the same rule, and selling never renews their grant. Consumables and materials with uncertain remaining supply have no standard resale offer. Goods freshly crafted or acquired at full supply may attract half-price offers, but the buyer must actually need that quantity. Special items still require an available willing trader; apply the same half-sale/full-trade rule to the agreed item valuation. Treasure such as gems has its stated trade value, without a second automatic half-price reduction.

All material bundles must name their actual contents. Ordinary d6 ingredients cost 12 coins; a d6 prepared healing-ingredient bundle costs 80. Other rare inputs need a quote. Materials must meet the recipe: a common bundle cannot become life salts by relabeling it. Recipes are still found, derived or granted through cards, not automatically available for coin purchase.

Gathering ingredients and crafting your own supplies can save coins. Before producing goods for sale, find a willing buyer and agree on the quantity and price with the DA. Allow time to gather materials and complete each recipe. The buyer’s needs determine how much they will purchase.

Shopping bundles and starting range

Bundles are convenience lists at the exact sum of their parts, with no discount or Bulk exemption. Each person still chooses what to carry.

  • Road essentials: 24 coins, 5 Bulk. Pack 3 + sleeping roll 4 + filled water

flask 3 + d8 food 9 + d6 lighting 5. One plain worn outfit is free.

  • Self-contained explorer: 31 coins, 7 Bulk. Road essentials + rope 5 and small

necessities 2. At Brawn −1, this alone fills capacity 7.

  • Road essentials plus lesser healing: 44 coins, 6 Bulk. Add a 20-coin d4 bottle.
  • Explorer plus lesser healing: 51 coins, 8 Bulk. Useful, but too much for a

Brawn −1 character without sharing a load or accepting a Speed penalty.

A spell light can replace a purchased lighting supply if the group accepts its limitations. Sharing rope, light and camp tools is a choice, not a free group inventory. Card-granted items remain part of carried Bulk even though they cost no coins at creation.

Agreed starting target: 50–70 coins after card grants. At 50, a character can buy road essentials, a lesser potion and retain 6 coins; at 70 that same choice leaves 26 for specialist purchases or reserves. The fully equipped explorer with a potion costs 51, so the low end requires a small tradeoff. This is a purchasing target; calculate the actual purse from the starting allocation below.

The @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.880380bcd80cfec6]{starting allocation} supplies base + ancestry + culture + background + class values, all within that target.

A recipe is the knowledge of how to make a particular thing. It tells you which knowledge or technique permits the work, what tools and materials you need, how long an attempt takes, and what the result produces. Gather its ingredients and use the technique described in the recipe.

Read the entry before beginning. A project may accumulate progress toward a completion target; a supply recipe may instead raise an existing inventory die. Follow the printed outcomes and limits. Starting crafting abilities provide their stated recipe choices; you can learn further compatible recipes through the appropriate ability or discover them during play.

Check how to learn the recipe and which technique to use for the work. Trail Workshop teaches its named recipe choices. Other formulas can be learned from teachers or discovery; gather their materials and equipment before beginning.

For every recipe, roll the crafting ability’s printed attribute at the end of an attempt. Work alone; there is no group crafting. Accumulate project progress until you meet the completion target. For supplies, the first inventory step from empty creates d4; later steps are d6, d8, d10, d12 and d20, up to the recipe’s cap. Check any carried material supply after each attempt. You must actually obtain the ingredients; prepare the finished stock through crafting. Recipes remain known for reuse. The plants and mixtures here are fictional game ingredients.

You call across a boundary, and something answers: paws on stone, a flicker of ancestral light, a shape unfolding from cold air. The creature acts through your attention. Its presence gives you choices, not a second independent turn.

Your summoning spell tells you which companions you can call. Find its category in Summon Selection and choose a creature whose rating is no higher than the spell allows. If the spell names a particular creature, use that creature’s profile. Keep the profile beside your sheet for its attributes and actions.

Summons are energy forms shaped to resemble creatures. They cannot receive healing and disappear at 0 HP without leaving a body. They occupy squares, block movement, take damage and can be pushed or grappled normally unless the profile says otherwise; energy form grants no automatic incorporeality or immunity.

Command the creature

Spend your Main Action to give one summon a Main Action and a Maneuver. Spend your Maneuver to give one summon a Maneuver and movement. Normal conversions apply. The Main-command package has no separate movement allowance: convert its Maneuver to movement if it needs to approach before attacking.

A summon receives at most one command on your turn. You can spend your Main Action on one creature and your Maneuver on another. A summoning spell's immediate free Main command counts as that creature's command for the turn.

Summoned creatures require your constant interaction and concentration to maintain their presence in reality. At the end of your turn, each of your summons that received no command during that turn disappears. Its immediate command when summoned counts for that turn.

An uncommanded summon does nothing. It does not follow, keep watch, alert you, continue a previous task, or take Reactions and opportunity attacks. Existing conditions, durations and passive defenses still operate. Resolve its turn-based timing on your turn. You cannot summon creatures that summon more creatures.

Keep the connection

A summon disappears beyond 6 squares from you, including after forced movement of either participant. It also disappears at 0 HP, or when you become unconscious or die. Its duration may end earlier. It leaves no permanent equipment or loot.

Measure the tether between the nearest occupied squares of controller and summon, using ordinary grid distance. At 6 squares the summon remains; beyond 6 it immediately disappears. The nearest square of a large form sets the distance.

Healing through a summon

When a summon uses a printed healing ability, you pay its SP cost once before resolution. You must have enough SP. The summon uses its own attribute and outcomes and still requires its command and action. It can heal an eligible other creature, but cannot receive healing. Ordinary unsummoned healers pay their own cost.

Give a useful order

“Attack that creature,” “defend this spot,” “move into cover,” and “help them cross” are clear intentions. The creature still needs the printed capability and enough commanded actions to carry them out. A previous order never buys activity next turn. Outside combat, you must continue directing a longer task for its full time.

Roll the creature's attack attribute, not your own, and read its player-facing attacker outcomes. When it is attacked, roll the defense attribute named by the incoming attack using the creature's value. Apply the profile's attack or defense Boons/Banes and resistance normally. There is never a second opposed roll.

The profiles below include only the summoned form's permitted capabilities. A monster's dramatic description does not grant its summoned form extra actions, active auras, independent attacks or skills.

Choose a creature, not another spell

Each summoning spell specifies its category, maximum eligible roster rating, placement and duration. Choose a listed profile in that category at or below the printed rating. The six families are Animal, Fey, Spirit, Elemental, Undead and Construct. Ratings 1, 3 and 7 identify the available profiles; learned spellbook pages determine which callings you can cast. A spell that names a particular profile uses that profile directly.

A category is an explicit bestiary tag. A ghost is not automatically selectable under both Spirit and Undead; its entry must say so. These are summoned forms, not permission to seize an existing creature or extract permanent equipment.

Summoned energy forms — approved October 16, 2026

A summon is shaped from energies to resemble and act like the chosen creature; it is not an actual physical creature brought into the scene. It cannot be healed. Its HP tracks how much damage the form can sustain. At 0 HP it disappears rather than leaving a body. The existing duration, tether and controller-disappearance rules still apply.

Tangibility — approved October 16, 2026: summoned forms occupy squares and block movement normally. They can take damage and be pushed or grappled normally unless their card explicitly says otherwise. Being made from energy does not automatically make a summon incorporeal or grant damage or control immunities.

This restriction concerns receiving healing. A summon with a printed healing ability can still heal an eligible other creature, with its controller paying the printed cost as described below. Ordinary unsummoned creatures keep their own healing rules. A printed harmful Life effect is damage, not healing.

Pay for activity

Summoned creatures require your constant interaction and concentration to maintain their presence in reality. At the end of your turn, each of your summons that received no command during that turn disappears. The immediate command granted when you summon a creature counts as its command for that turn.

Agreed: an uncommanded summon does nothing. It does not follow, keep watch, alert its controller, continue attacking, search, help or perform a standing order. It takes no independent Reaction, including an opportunity attack. A prior order never pays for another turn. Outside combat the same rule prevents unattended work, scouting or guard duty; the controller must actively spend the required time and actions directing it.

  • Controller spends Main Action: one summon receives Main Action + Maneuver.
  • Controller spends Maneuver: one summon receives Maneuver + movement.
  • A summon receives at most one command on the controller’s turn. The controller

may spend these two actions on different summons.

  • Normal conversions apply: Main → Maneuver → movement. There is no separate free

movement grant in the Main-command package. For example, convert its Maneuver to movement to approach, then spend Main on an attack.

  • A newly summoned creature receives the summoning spell’s immediate free Main

command. That is its command for this turn; it cannot also receive a paid one.

  • Resolve the granted activity on the controller’s turn. It cannot be banked for

an enemy turn. No summon chains and no independent summon turns.

Commanding has no roll. Any permitted attack or task uses the summon profile’s printed procedure. A command is not automatic success or a way to invent a skill.

Healing through a summon

When a summoned creature uses a healing ability, its controller pays the ability’s printed SP cost instead of the summon. Pay once, before resolving the ability, from the controller’s SP reserve. The controller must have enough SP or the ability cannot be used. The summon still uses its own printed attribute and healing outcomes; its command and action requirements are unchanged.

For example, the Moon Hart’s Battle Mending costs its controller 3 SP, then the player rolls the hart’s Reason for 5/10/15 healing. The hart does not also pay 3 SP. An ordinary unsummoned healer continues to pay its own cost.

Orders in ordinary language

These examples describe intent, not a new menu of abilities granted to every creature.

OrderExecution within the paid package
Attack that creatureUse a permitted attack. A Main command can convert its Maneuver to movement to approach first.
Defend that spotA Maneuver command supplies movement and Defend, if the profile permits Defend. It does not grant free attacks at intruders.
Move there / follow meUse only the granted movement, with legal routes and endpoints. Following stops when that movement ends.
Move and hideMove to real concealment, then use the profile’s printed hiding action if the remaining budget permits it. No automatic Hidden.
Move and keep watchMove, then use its printed observation action if affordable. It can report what it notices during that commanded activity; no continuing lookout afterward.
Help themUse Aid or a printed support ability, if permitted and affordable.
Fetch or handle thisUse permitted movement and interaction; anatomy, reach, carried Bulk and action costs still apply.
Track thisUse the profile’s tracking procedure and available senses. The command does not grant tracking expertise.

If a creature lacks the required capability or the package lacks the necessary actions, it cannot complete that order. A longer task needs continued commands and the printed activity time; one spoken instruction never buys hours of labor.

What still happens without a command

Until it disappears at the end of your turn, the creature remains present and can be damaged or forcibly moved. Existing conditions, durations, tether checks and already-resolved effects continue normally. These are consequences, not permission for new activity. A previous Defend benefit lasts only to its printed expiry; it does not renew itself.

Six-square tether — approved October 16, 2026

Measure ordinary grid distance between the nearest occupied squares of the controller and summon. Diagonals count normally as one square. The summon remains present at a distance of 6 squares; if the nearest distance exceeds 6, it immediately disappears. Voluntary or forced movement of either participant can break the tether.

For example, a large summon remains present with its nearest square 6 squares away and its farthest square 7 away. If its nearest square becomes 7 squares away, it disappears. Neither creature’s center nor farthest occupied square sets the distance.

The summon profile must anchor any “your turn” duration or condition tick to the controller’s turn. Passive defenses such as resistance remain applicable. Do not import automatic attacks, active auras or triggered abilities from a monster entry without an explicit summon-profile procedure consistent with command-only activity.

Bestiary selection

The summon selection provides 73 entries, covering all six categories at tiers 1, 3 and 7. Each prints HP, all six attributes, attack and target-defense attributes, movement, footprint, senses, resistance, the no-healing rule, command options and restrictions. Category or CV alone never authorizes a creature.

The creature procedure and summon selection document the permitted command activities. Use the approved tether measurement above and the @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.3292b6a49dcf7236]{moving-group placement rules} where relevant. Use the entry itself, not a monster’s narrative tactics as a standing order. No activity, alerts or independent Reactions without the permitted command.

When the controller falls: summons disappear when their controller becomes unconscious or dies. Players roll their creatures’ printed attack and defense attributes; see @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.f5003d6e49eeed0c]{session resolution}.

Every survived incident that brought a hero to 0 HP leaves a descriptive scar. Choose it with the player after danger passes. Use these prompts to describe what the hero remembers or carries with them. A scar never adds a mechanical penalty or benefit.

What happenedA possible lasting reminder
Steel or clawsA pale line across the shoulder; a nick through an eyebrow
Fire or lightningA silver streak of hair; branching marks on the arm
ColdWhite fingertips; a patch of frost-pale skin
Crushing forceA seam along the jaw; a story about the shield that broke
Mental magicA recurring dream; a phrase you remember when frightened
Radiant magicA bright fleck in the iris; a sun-shaped mark
Life-draining magicA white lock of hair; a shadow beneath the old injury
A desperate rescueA companion's name tattooed beside the mark

The player decides how a remembered event affects their hero's personality. Do not impose trauma, disability or involuntary behavior as the price of surviving. A chosen scar cannot justify an automatic Bane, lost action or movement penalty.

Record the scar, the incident and who helped you survive. No severity or treatment track is needed. A later adventure may give the mark new meaning. The @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.9303127ab1b28c3b]{recovery rules} govern HP, stabilization, death rolls and Grit.

Driving Opening I. Maneuver. Choose one visible creature. Before your turn ends, your next Main Action melee weapon attack against it pushes that creature directly away from your attack position, 1 square on Standard or 2 squares on Strong. Resolve collisions normally. Apply the push only to the chosen creature on that attack. Reusing this technique replaces its unused effect.

Interpose I. Reaction. After an adjacent ally rolls defense, before applying physical damage from that attack, reduce that damage by 1 after resistance. You must be able to reach the ally. No roll.

Shield Bash I. Main Action · Brawn. Attack one adjacent creature with your shield for 1/2/3 physical damage. On Standard or Strong, push it 1 square directly away. Resolve collisions normally.

Sheltering Guard I. Maneuver. Choose one willing adjacent ally. Until your next turn starts it gains 1 Boon on ranged defenses while adjacent. Reusing this technique replaces its previous effect. No roll.

At the table

Use Measured Cut II as your Main Action. Driving Opening prepares its push with your Maneuver; Interpose or Step Between protects an ally with your Reaction. Shield Bash is an alternative Main Action. Wear light armor and hold hammer and shield; free a hand before manipulating another item.

Wild Harvest I. Main Action · 1 hour · Knowledge. Search an accessible area for food or drinkable water. The DA defines the area and confirms a plausible source before you roll. Raise one Food Bundle or Water Flask of the chosen type by 1/2/3 supply die steps, maximum d8. An empty supply starts at d4 on the first step. Gentle Hand I. Maneuver · Reason. Reassure one nonmagical animal within 2 squares that can perceive you and add 1/2/3 progress toward calming its fear. Spend a Maneuver with a receptive animal or 1 minute per attempt with a wary or agitated one. Find an approach it can respond to in the circumstances.

Field Dressing I. Main Action, with a free hand and bandaging: reduce an adjacent patient’s Bleeding by 2, minimum 0, without HP restoration or a first-aid attempt. Alternatively spend 10 minutes and roll Knowledge to restore 3/5/7 HP to a patient within reach, consuming its first-aid attempt.

Field Dressing II. Field Dressing’s first aid restores 4/6/8 HP; its immediate bandaging reduces Bleeding by 3.

Patient Care I. Maneuver. With suitable water, blankets or other supplies and a free hand, reduce temporary Burning or Freezing on one adjacent patient by 2, minimum 0. No roll, HP restoration or first-aid attempt.

Trail Warning I. Reaction. When a visible natural hazard begins to threaten a companion within 3 squares, before its avoidance roll, warn it. If it can perceive you, that roll gains 1 Boon. The hazard must be something you can observe, such as shifting footing or a falling branch. Once per hazard event.

At the table

Mend uses a Main Action and 1 SP. Growth I supplies a free attack cantrip and Entangle. Use the universal Sustain Spell Maneuver for an active spell that calls for it; it costs 0 SP. The universal Opportunity Attack is available with a free hand. Field Dressing II improves the same daily first-aid allowance, rather than granting another treatment. Keep supplies accessible.

All universal actions remain available. An improvement changes its named technique; keep its benefits together on the sheet. First aid starts available, with no death marks or scars.

Your learned techniques

Mend and Fit I. Main Action, with tools and a suitable brace or fastening: temporarily secure one damaged nonmagical item within reach so it can support its ordinary stationary load until your next turn ends. It gains no HP and cannot attack or protect from attacks while broken. Alternatively work for 10 minutes and roll Knowledge for 1/2/3 progress toward repairing an item that retains enough structure.

Mend and Fit II. Mend and Fit’s repair work adds 1/3/4 progress. Its temporary brace lasts 1 minute unless the item moves or receives further damage.

Smoke in a Bottle I. 1 hour · Knowledge, with alchemical tools and one purchased batch of smoke ingredients. Add 1/2/3 progress toward target 3 to prepare one smoke flask. Maneuver: throw a prepared flask to a visible point within 4 squares, consuming it. Smoke fills a 1-square-radius area until your next turn ends and blocks sight through it. No throwing roll.

Catch the Failure I. Reaction. When a visible component within reach begins to fail during a nonmagical task, use tools in hand to arrest it before the consequence resolves. Give the worker 1 Boon on the associated roll to prevent injury or material loss, if such a roll is possible. Once per distinct failure event; this does not improve the task’s progress roll or reverse damage already applied.

Read the Evidence I. Main Action · Reason. Examine one accessible clue within reach; add 1/2/3 progress toward a concrete question about it. Searching a scene instead takes 10 minutes per attempt. You may also recall a relevant fact about a subject or reliable description: 1 minute, Knowledge, 1/2/3 progress toward a question set before rolling.

Read the Evidence II. Read the Evidence adds 1/3/4 progress to examination, scene searches and recall.

Survey the Ground I. Maneuver · Reason. Study one visible approach within 6 squares; add 1/2/3 progress toward identifying its usable footing and visible hazards. Surveying a whole site takes 10 minutes per attempt instead. Concealed threats require evidence to discover.

Portents I. Learn True Strike, Guidance.

Portents II. Learn Augury, Intuitions.

At the table

Spot the Leverage prepares an ally with a Maneuver. True Strike is a Main Action weapon attack using its spell rules; Oren holds a melee weapon and keeps the other hand free for casting. Catch the Failure supplies a situational Reaction around a failing item; Opportunity Attack remains available. Tools, materials and a place to work are still needed for Craft techniques.

Action: Maneuver · Attribute: None — no roll

Target / range / shape: One corner of your square; each creature in the four squares that share that corner and are in line of effect.

Choose a corner of your square and spark a brief flare of gas there. Each creature in the four squares that share that corner, including you, is pushed 2 squares directly away from that corner. A creature in more than one of those squares is pushed once. The spark does not provoke opportunity attacks. Resolve the push as forced movement; normal collision rules apply.

Duration: Immediate.

Equipment / acquisition: A free hand for casting.

This is a spell costing 0 SP, usable once on your turn. Its casting does not provoke opportunity attacks.

At the table

Fire Bolt provides a free Main Action attack; Flame II adds Burning Hands and Heat Metal. Deliberate Spark is a Maneuver that can also push allies and yourself, so choose its corner carefully. Air I supplies Feather Fall as a Reaction. Both hands begin free. The two capacity paths add 6 SP, producing 13 maximum SP; learning them is not a separate refill.

All universal actions remain available. An improvement changes its named technique; keep its benefits together on the sheet. First aid starts available, with no death marks or scars.

Glossary

Ability. A learned technique, spell or other capability with its own procedure. “Card” refers to that rules entry, whether printed on a card or in this book.

Action. Something a character chooses to do. An action can call for a roll; a roll itself is not an extra action. A Main Action is a specific part of the turn budget.

Attribute. One of Brawn, Fortitude, Agility, Guile, Knowledge or Reason. Add only the attribute called for by the action or DA.

Benefit. A useful additional advantage, including the extra consequence of a natural 666. Apply the stated Strong outcome as well.

Boon / Bane. An extra die that changes which three dice you retain. Boons and Banes cancel before applying their net cap.

Bulk. An item's inventory load. Capacity and carried Bulk determine encumbrance.

Class. Your hero’s training at level 1. Your class offers starting disciplines and signature choices at levels 1, 3 and 7.

Complication. An additional problem that does not erase progress already earned.

Condition. A named state with defined effects and removal. A condition's rating may measure severity, duration or both.

Consequence. What is at stake in an uncertain attempt. Establish it before rolling.

DA. Dungeon Architect, the participant who presents and adjudicates the world.

Discipline. A field of study with four paths or spellbooks. Your culture, background and class each supply one starting discipline. An additional discipline costs the 1, 2 or 3 DP printed for your class.

DP. Development Points, spent to study disciplines and learn entries. Start with 10 + Guile + Knowledge + Reason, plus explicit benefits. Gain 6 + the new level at each later level. Save unspent points.

DR. Damage reduction. Armor DR is physical resistance, applied after the attack outcome.

Dying. A player character's state at 0 HP before stabilization or recovery. Further damage at 0 causes an immediate death roll; surviving the incident leaves a descriptive scar.

Effect. A change produced by a rule. It might be immediate damage, movement, a condition or a continuing benefit. Its duration does not repeat instant damage.

Evasion / Threat. A creature's printed dice adjustments to player attacks / player defenses. They are Boons or Banes, not added numerical totals.

Free attack. An attack granted by a specific rule without spending an action. It cannot trigger another free attack.

Grit. A lifetime reserve gained once at levels 1/3/7. Spend one to return to half maximum HP, rounded up; it never refreshes.

Hidden. A universal concealed state, maintained by actual circumstances. Attacking or openly revealing yourself ends it.

HP. Current capacity to keep going. Record current and maximum separately.

Inventory die. A supply's remaining uncertainty. Roll after use; step down on 1.

Death. Three failures on death rolls kill unless Grit or an ability intervenes immediately. The player can describe their hero’s Last Words.

Maneuver. A smaller action used for movement techniques, setup, support and practical tasks.

Passive. A capability that requires no action unless its text says otherwise.

Reaction. Your limited response to a stated trigger. An ordinary defense roll is not itself a Reaction.

Treatment allowance. One attempt per recipient between safe overnight rests, shared across First Aid and learned treatments.

Resistance. Reduction to a matching damage type; highest source, maximum 3. Life resistance also reduces magical healing and potions.

Safe place. A location the DA judges suitable for spending saved DP. Brief and Night’s Rests have their own time and safety requirements.

Signature. An ability you choose from your class at level 1, 3 or 7.

Stability. Resistance to the distance of forced movement. Default 0, cap 3. It does not reduce damage, Prone or other conditions.

Learning. Learn the entries of an ability path or the sections of a spellbook in order. Check the listed DP and level requirement. Mark each spell taught by a section you learn.

Sustain. A Maneuver costing 0 SP. Sustain one spell at a time, as its text directs. A fixed duration continues for its stated time; moving a directed effect uses its printed action.

Scar. A descriptive reminder of surviving an incident at 0 HP; no mechanical penalties or treatment track.

Keep notes between sessions

Write down unfinished business, promises and discoveries the company might return to. When the group makes a ruling you expect to use again, note it where everyone can find it.

Survival at a glance

When you fall to 0 HP, you enter Dying, fall prone and lose consciousness. Roll Fortitude at the start of each Dying turn and immediately after each damaging event while already at 0 HP. Weak adds one failure, Strong adds one success and Standard changes neither. Use only the result band, including on triples. Three failures mean death. Three successes stabilize you at 0 HP. An adjacent ally can stabilize you with a Maneuver. Clear both tallies on stabilization or recovery above 0 HP. Spend Grit for half maximum HP, rounded up, even after the third failure.

These conventions apply to the current catalog.

Learn, declare, resolve

Each nonmagical path teaches an ability I, then II and III improve that same ability. Those effects add together unless a new total replaces an earlier total. The fourth entry, at level 3, teaches a distinct ability; the next two improve it. The seventh entry is a level-7 mastery. Sequential prices are 1/2/2/3/4/4/5 DP. North develops a Main Action, west a Maneuver, east a Reaction, and south a distinctive capability. Reactions may be used outside combat. Every hero can make basic melee and ranged attacks. Arms and Marksmanship develop those fighting skills further.

A magical discipline opens four spellbooks. Each book follows seven sequential sections for 1/2/2/3/4/4/5 DP, with gates 1/1/1/3/3/3/7. Sections I–IV each teach two spells; V, VI and VII each teach one spell. The seventh section is mastery. Spell 1 costs 0 SP to cast. Spellcraft provides Soul Capacity, Mind Capacity and Recovery training alongside the Channeling book. Capacity increases add to one shared SP pool.

Masteries follow their own path’s level-3 studies. Both martial and magical paths culminate in one level-7 mastery.

Choose class signatures at their milestones without spending DP.

Declare a card before rolling. Roll 3d6 plus its one printed attribute with the normal Boon/Bane rules. No skill bonus, weapon damage die or extra attribute damage. A no-roll card simply does what it says. Rolled cards give their Weak, Standard and Strong results in the text; a shared 1/2/3 progression always follows that order.

Range uses squares. “Adjacent” means within one square with an actual accessible path. Visible targets still require an attack path. A player area/multitarget attack uses one roll with the worst applicable net Boon/Bane situation. NPC attacks give each affected player a defense roll. A printed NPC defense attribute is a choice for that attack, not the attribute a player attacker rolls.

Costs and time

Main Action, Maneuver, Reaction, Movement and Passive are distinct labels. A long activity prints its full time; “Main Action” does not allow an hour of treatment in one turn. No-roll does not mean free. A triggered Passive effect spends no action unless stated. A Reaction spends the one available Reaction.

Instant damage or displacement occurs once. A named temporary condition continues under the condition rules, not forever because the attack’s duration is Instant. “Once per turn” means your turn unless a different creature’s turn is named. “Once per round” resets at the start of your next turn. “Scene” means one continuous situation; a brief pause does not reset it.

Healing costs 1/2/4 SP by tier, paid before the roll; the caster must have the SP. Requires a free hand. Healing resistance is Life resistance; minimum 1 applies only when HP is missing. No healing above maximum. Potions use their own fixed value and inventory die, with no spell outcome roll or caster cost.

Equipment and grants

A grant supplies a missing ordinary item on acquisition. It does not supply another compatible weapon just because another attack was learned, and selling the item does not reactivate a past grant. Ordinary melee and ranged weapons each use Bulk 1. Their names and appearance add no damage. Special equipment adds only printed effects. A requirement without a grant may require treasure or coins; flag that in starter advice.

Bonus and effect language

Same-kind numeric bonuses use the highest. Boons/Banes stack normally. Numbered conditions stack where meaningful; repeated binary Prone does not become Prone 2. Free attacks never trigger more free attacks. A free attack does not consume actions, but only the granting effect determines what attack is permitted.

Displacements use the shared movement rules. “Move without provoking” does not allow walking through walls or occupied standing creatures. Teleportation is explicit. Flavor never silently grants flight, telepathy, armor, a second damage type or immunity.

Proposed sorting types

Attack, Defense, Movement, Control, Recovery, Utility, Skill, Magic, Crafting, Training and Signature are tags, not additional rules. Multiple tags are allowed. Action cost is indexed separately. Ancestry, Origin, Discipline, Equipment and Recipe identify record kinds rather than learned-card prerequisites.

Printed layout later: numbered diamond top left, name top center, discipline icons top right. Type, action, range, outcomes, duration and limits remain visible. Color can support the tier but may never replace its number.

A different kind of expertise

Use the attribute printed on the ability. Learning an unusual attack does not replace every attack’s attribute. No skill modifier is added.

Beast forms keep your own HP, scars and attributes; they are not disposable HP pools. Use the form’s printed actions and equipment restrictions. The new cards state how to enter and leave a form, so the table does not need a monster stat block.

Noncombat cards should be read as things a person can do. Correct ordinary action still needs no roll when no consequence is at stake. An expert adds an opportunity, useful detail or reliability; owning the card is not a license for everyone else to stop thinking creatively.

Imagine it, then resolve it

Agreed October 13, 2026. Every card begins with narrative text describing what using it looks, sounds or feels like. One vivid sentence is enough for a simple ability; a more elaborate ability may deserve more. Address the player and make an action or experience imaginable. This applies to universal actions, signatures, shared abilities and the other character, equipment and recipe records.

Follow the narrative with a distinct Rules section. Only this section establishes mechanical permissions and effects. State who acts, the target, action or full time, attribute or no-roll instruction, prerequisites, costs, outcomes, duration and limits as applicable. A triggered effect states its trigger and resolution timing. A movement effect states its distance and legal endpoints. A benefit states its recipients and expiry. Do not bury any of these in the narrative.

For example, “You tie the knot without looking, then test it with a tug” evokes experience. “While climbing, secure one held rope at a reachable suitable anchor without a separate action; a free hand is required” is the adjudicated rule. Narrative does not imply an extra sense, free item, automatic success or magical power.

Keep acquisition facts in Rules too. An origin’s memory prompt belongs above Rules; its paired discipline/card grant belongs below. For an item, describe the experience of handling it, then specify its actual additive effects and use requirements.

Development breadth

Each discipline has four sequential paths. The first three learned entries build one ability; the endpoint adds a new capability at level 3. Combined abilities require every exact endpoint, level 7 and 3/4/5 DP for two/three/four disciplines. Class signatures keep class-and-level requirements. See @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.c160c7b39d6731f7]{learning}.

Concrete language review

Bruce’s correction, October 13, 2026: a narrative heading and an evocative slogan are insufficient. Describe what the character actually does and what becomes visible, audible or felt. “You reach for tomorrow’s sky” leaves the action unspecified. Reaching through a tear in the air, pulling out a clump of weather and tossing it onto the ground gives the player an action to imagine. Passive expertise may instead describe the practiced habit or observation that produces its benefit.

Read the narrative independently of the title and rules. Could a player describe that action to the table? Does it suggest the effect this card actually supplies? Avoid replacing a specific action with a promise, maxim or mysterious metaphor. Sensory detail should make the action clearer; it should not imply an extra power.

Read the rules in the order someone uses them: choose the target, meet requirements, pay the action/cost, make any roll, apply the result, then track its expiry. Explain unusual dice operations on the card. “Lowest retained die” is not sufficient: say which dice are examined after Boons/Banes and whether the printed numbers or modified total matter. Put separate effects in separate sentences or bullets. Show Weak, Standard and Strong rather than compressing a whole procedure into unexplained slashes.

Finally, read every field against the card’s purpose. A swimming card must not carry a recipient treatment limit; an area card should say which creatures it affects rather than recite rules for unrelated target shapes. Structural checks cannot perform this editorial review, and passing them must not be presented as proof that wording is clear.

Table and VTT resolution

Review revision, October 13, 2026. Read a card in this order: check permission and equipment, declare choices and targets, pay its action and costs, roll if called for, apply the complete outcome, then mark its duration. Choices of damage type are made before rolling; no ability in this revision inspects an individual die to select a second unrelated effect.

A card's full activity time overrides its combat action label. Crafting and using a crafted supply are separate procedures. Do not reduce an hour of work to a Main Action because the action field uses that label for sorting.

Outcome bullets are complete results, not cumulative instructions: apply only the rolled bullet. Where it says “also” or “both benefits,” apply those stated benefits as well. Instant damage happens once; numbered conditions then follow their own resolve-and-decay rules. A duration field never makes attack damage recur.

For an area described as “within N squares,” every selected square must be in range. A connected placed area uses edge-sharing squares. Rectangles extend in a chosen grid direction from a square adjacent to the caster; choose their footprint before rolling. Include allies only where the card targets every creature. Resolve multiple displacements in an order the acting player chooses, using the shared collision rules; unresolved moving-group geometry remains a DA ruling.

Use Push for movement directly away from the source, Pull for movement directly toward it, and Slide for movement in any direction. State the maximum distance in squares and print any special source point, path or destination restrictions.

Use the character's existing roll for a reaction that modifies that roll. A card which grants Basic Melee directs its recipient to the Basic Melee card; “no separate roll” never makes the granted attack automatic Strong. A player attack still gets one roll and never causes a second player defense roll.

A Boon to defense against forced movement applies to an attack's ordinary defense if that attack can move the defender. It never creates an extra defense against no-roll displacement. Cards that depend on a defense roll do nothing when the normal player-attacker rule supplies no such roll.

VTT records should store action, full time, attribute or delegated roll, targets, range, shape, choices, outcomes, equipment, cost, condition rating, duration anchor, and use limit separately. Track a continuing benefit as one effect with its stated expiry, not a fresh bonus every time the token is selected. Narrative, physical plausibility, willing participation and DA judgments stay visible to the people playing; do not turn them into extra automated saves.

Shared access and condition combinations

Every class can learn a shared ability by meeting its printed level and discipline requirements and paying its price. Beginning another discipline costs the 1, 2 or 3 DP printed for the hero’s class. Class signatures retain their printed class requirements.

An ability that targets every creature meeting a condition affects the whole eligible group within its printed range and shape. The condition remains unless the ability explicitly changes or removes it. Player-selected activation order supports one character setting up another character's payoff; normal condition timing continues to apply.

Class signature standard

Agreed: signatures define their class and are slightly more powerful than shared cards at the same tier. Give each choice a useful, recognizable advantage: better action efficiency, reliability, scope, positioning or a distinctive permission. A vivid name alone does not establish that advantage. Compare the whole procedure, including costs, targets and limits, rather than only damage.

Each milestone at levels 1, 3 and 7 offers one independent signature choice without spending DP. Write its complete action, target, costs and effects on its own card. A signature may add a short benefit when the hero also knows another named signature. Such an interaction does not grant that other signature or make it a prerequisite; refer to its name instead of repeating its rules.

Signature records retain Type: Signature and use Tags for their functional roles; action cost remains a separate field.

Focused Maneuver development

Agreed direction: use Maneuvers for special positioning, setup and support. Keep ordinary movement simple; do not introduce movement-priced ability activations or add variable-cost/conversion cards merely to fill a catalog category. Independent options span all three tiers.

Stability and movement

All pushes, pulls and throws of creatures use @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.3292b6a49dcf7236]{Stability}, including additional creatures struck in a collision chain. Distances on cards are before Stability. Other riders still apply when displacement is reduced to 0. Voluntary movement, projectile range, obstacle progress and grapple reduction are not reduced by Stability. Any exception must be explicit on the card.

November 19 advancement DP

After level 1, gain 6 + the new level in DP, plus explicit trait benefits. Level 2 grants 8 DP and level 3 grants 9. Heroes who already advanced gain 2 DP for each level they earned after level 1. See #368.

Agreed targets: four player characters are the reference party; typical combat about 4 rounds, hard about 6, extreme about 10. Typical reasonably prepared parties should have roughly a 20–30% chance of at least one hero falling to 0 HP without a healer, 5–15% with one. These are feel targets, not mandatory outcomes for every battle.

Proposed budget procedure

Define B(L) as the calibrated standard encounter budget for four characters of level L. For N characters of the same level:

Budget = B(L) × N / 4 × difficulty multiplier.

Proposed multipliers: easy 0.75, standard 1.00, hard 1.50, extreme 2.00. Round the final budget to a convenient whole CV. These multipliers are starting fixtures, not verified mappings to encounter duration. An extreme encounter must not simply be declared a ten-round fight because its budget doubled.

For mixed levels, use sum(B(character level) / 4), then multiply by difficulty. This preserves each character’s calibrated contribution rather than rounding the party’s average level. Budget is the sum of participating enemies’ CV. Waves and reinforcements count; terrain and mission objectives require separate review.

Arithmetic example only: if future calibration establishes B(1)=40, three level-1 characters receive a standard budget of 30; five receive 50. A hard fight for five would be 75. Forty is a demonstration input, not an assigned level-1 budget.

Proposed creature estimate, followed by testing

Start with CV estimate = sqrt(E × O) × U, normalized so a chosen reference creature has the desired reference CV.

  • E = expected attacks needed to defeat it using the reference party’s actual

attack outcomes, hit effects, resistances and relevant control. Do not divide HP by a single raw damage number that ignores minimum damage.

  • O = expected effective HP damage per round against that party, counting actual

targets, action economy and healing. Use recorded outcome probabilities and attack/defense attributes, not an assumed universal success rate.

  • U = an explicit provisional adjustment for disabling effects, movement, unusual

senses, reach, summoning or other advantages not represented by E and O. Start at 1 for an ordinary damage-only creature; document every other value.

This is a seed metric, not a final algorithm. Zero-damage controllers cannot receive zero CV: evaluate their contribution in a mixed encounter instead of applying this formula blindly. Healing loops, area attacks and incapacitation can make the simple estimate unreliable. Record uncertainty rather than publishing false precision.

Calibration sequence for the bestiary

1. Build a few ordinary melee/ranged creatures with full printed attack and defense attributes, HP, resistances, Stability, actions and outcomes. 2. Test actual level-1 parties with documented supplies and healing access. 3. Fit B(1) and creature CV to duration, falls to 0 HP, defeat risk and action loss. 4. Test 3-, 4- and 5-character parties and easy/hard/extreme multipliers. Include open and obstructed terrain; party-size scaling may need an enemy-count warning. 5. Add control, healing and summons one feature at a time; refine U or replace the seed metric if it fails. Then repeat at levels 3 and 7 and intermediate levels.

Until those tests exist, CV and B(L) remain uncalibrated. The procedure is ready to support bestiary development; numerical encounter guarantees are not.

Bestiary seed worksheet

The bestiary encounter draft now supplies explicit reference attacks, enumerated probabilities, utility factors and a proposed B(L)=32+8L testing grid. These are authoring seeds, not the completed calibration described above. Every creature’s CV can be recomputed by the bestiary audit.
